It accepts errors as well as warnings on purpose: SH168's `unknown-field` is exactly the class that otherwise sends people to `|| true`.
  <br>**Deliberately a project file and not an instance setting.** What is acceptable is a property of *this repository's* content and belongs in review beside it, and the thing it protects — the exit code — is the CLI's. `GET /agent/verify` keeps reporting every finding, which is right: an agent asking "what is wrong here" should be told, including about the parts a human already signed off. Only the gate subtracts. 15 network-free tests ([verify-baseline.test.mjs](../cli/test/verify-baseline.test.mjs)).

- **SH143** — **A verify run scoped to what changed** ([ShAgentVerifyScope](../shio-app/src/main/java/com/viglet/shio/api/agent/verify/ShAgentVerifyScope.java), [ShAgentVerifyService](../shio-app/src/main/java/com/viglet/shio/api/agent/verify/ShAgentVerifyService.java)). The pass read every post in every readable site — right for CI, and roughly a hundred times more work than the call an agent makes after writing three pages. `?folder=` (a subtree), `?address=` (named posts, comma-separated) and `?since=` (an SH88 cursor) narrow it; the three **union** rather than intersect, because each names something the caller wants looked at. Also `shio verify --folder/--address/--since` and three arguments on `shio_verify`, which is the caller this was built for.
  <br>**Why it is a refactor and not a filter.** Two rules ask cross-cutting questions — is another published post claiming this URL, does this link land anywhere in the site — and one asks whether a folder holds content. A scoped run that answered any of them from its own subjects would invent defects that are not there (`link-unresolved` for every link out of the scope, `empty-folder` for every folder it did not look inside) and miss the one that is: a duplicate whose twin is outside. So the **subjects** narrow and the **indexes stay whole**, built from id/url/state projections — one query per site, no entities, none of the cost a full read pass is expensive for ([findUrlIndexBySiteId](../shio-app/src/main/java/com/viglet/shio/persistence/repository/post/ShPostUnifiedRepository.java), `findFolderIdsWithPosts`, [findParentFolderIds](../shio-app/src/main/java/com/viglet/shio/persistence/repository/folder/ShFolderRepository.java)). `duplicate-url` became a per-subject lookup against the index for the same reason, and on a full pass emits exactly what it always did.
  <br>**A subset never reads as a full pass.** A scoped run sets `partial` and describes itself in `scope` (both absent on a full run — a flag that is always present is a flag nobody reads), the terse header carries them, and a `since` feed with more entries than fitted is a `note` rather than a silent cut. A `folder=` that resolves to something that is not a folder is a teaching **400**, not an empty green run: a scope that covered nothing while answering `ok` is the most dangerous false green there is. 9 tests, three of them about what scoping must not break ([ShAgentVerifyScopeTest](../shio-app/src/test/java/com/viglet/shio/api/agent/verify/ShAgentVerifyScopeTest.java)).
  <br>**Budget:** `mcp.tools.list.total` 2160 → 2200 — the one raise on that file where the schema cost is repaid inside the same feature, since the arguments exist so the tool can stop returning a whole-instance report. Two rounds of trimming went first.

**Follow-ups — the block's last four: pixels, a durable record, the route proof, and the handoff**

- **SH102** — **Visual snapshot + diff** ([snapshot.mjs](../cli/src/snapshot.mjs), [commands/snapshot.mjs](../cli/src/commands/snapshot.mjs), `shio snapshot`). The block's optional last piece, and the one whose *framing* was most of the design: it was specified from the start as an artifact for the human handoff rather than an agent input, so that nobody would mistake it for the primary verification path. Everything about the implementation follows from taking that seriously. 15 browser-free tests ([snapshot.test.mjs](../cli/test/snapshot.test.mjs)) — a test that launched Chromium would be testing Playwright, and what needed pinning was the baseline rotation, the two comparison resolutions and the exit code.
  <br>**A visual change exits 0.** A page looking different is usually the change you just made, and a command that failed on that is the command people wrap in `|| true` — which would take the *evidence* down with the gate. `--fail-on-change` is the opt-in gate; `--accept` moves the baseline deliberately rather than as a side effect of looking at it, and the displaced image is kept as `<slug>.prev.png`, because the artifact a human wants is before-and-after, not "after plus a percentage".
  <br>**Playwright is an optional dynamic import.** `@viglet/shio` is installed to author content, and taxing every install with a browser-automation library for a command the roadmap itself calls optional is the wrong trade; absent, it is a teaching error naming the two commands that fix it (P6) and pointing at `shio digest` as the check the agent should be using anyway. `pixelmatch` + `pngjs` are optional in the same way, and this is where the honesty rule lands: with them the comparison is per-pixel and reports a ratio; without them it compares **bytes** and reports `null` rather than a fabricated magnitude, because a made-up number is exactly what a caller would build a threshold on. The output names which of the two answers it gave, since "unchanged" from a byte comparison and from a pixel comparison are different claims.
  <br>**Determinism is the feature, not the polish.** A comparison whose baseline moves on its own is worse than none: it reports a change every run, the reader learns the output is noise, and the real regression goes unread. So the capture pins the viewport and timezone, forces `reducedMotion`, injects a stylesheet killing animations, transitions and the text caret, scrolls the page once so lazy images load, and awaits `document.fonts`. Every line that looks fussy is one of those. Baselines live in `shio/snapshots/` beside `shio/post-types/` and `shio/content/` so a reviewer sees the image in the diff — that PNGs are heavy in git is a real cost and one more reason the command is opt-in.
  <br>**The manifest still reports `visualSnapshot: false`, and that is not an oversight.** The flag advertises what the *agent surface* can do; there is no endpoint and no MCP tool, so an agent reading `true` would hunt for a call that does not exist. Unblocks **SH187**, which is this instrument scoped for the other reader.

**Follow-ups — a durable record, the route proof, and the handoff a human reads**

- **SH144** — **The durable incident feed** ([ShAgentIncident](../shio-app/src/main/java/com/viglet/shio/persistence/model/agent/ShAgentIncident.java), [ShAgentIncidentStore](../shio-app/src/main/java/com/viglet/shio/api/agent/diagnostics/ShAgentIncidentStore.java), [v2026.3.12.yaml](../shio-app/src/main/resources/db/changelog/v2026.3.12.yaml), `incidents` on [ShAgentChanges](../shio-app/src/main/java/com/viglet/shio/api/agent/dto/ShAgentChanges.java)). SH103's window was in memory and said so — which was the right answer for a first pass and an admission: "was anything failing while I was away" is a question about a period a ring buffer may no longer cover, and a restart answered it with silence. Now the record is a table, and one `since=` answers what changed *and* what broke. 11 tests ([ShAgentDurableIncidentTest](../shio-app/src/test/java/com/viglet/shio/api/agent/diagnostics/ShAgentDurableIncidentTest.java)), plus two of SH103's own rewritten because the behaviour they pinned is deliberately gone.
  <br>**Folding is what makes the table affordable.** SH103's objection was a write on the failure path plus a retention policy. A row is keyed by *what went wrong* (`kind`, `subject`, `message`), not by each occurrence, so one broken webhook retried for a month is one row with a count — the table grows with the number of distinct problems, which is a number an operator wants to see anyway. The pathological case (a subject carrying an id) is bounded by `shio.agent.diagnostics.max-rows`, and what the cap drops is visible through `since` moving forward rather than being quietly forgotten.
  <br>**The write cannot make things worse.** It runs in **`REQUIRES_NEW`**, because several callers are inside a transaction that is about to roll back — the 5xx filter's request, a scheduled publish that threw — and a row enlisted in that transaction would be destroyed by the very failure it exists to record. And it **never throws**: anything the persistence layer raises is caught and logged, since a diagnostics store that turned a webhook timeout into a 500 would be strictly worse than forgetting the incident. A failed write is counted, and the payload says the record is incomplete — the case that matters most, because the likeliest reason a write failed is that the database was itself what was failing. The in-memory buffer therefore stays: it is what is left when the store is unavailable.
  <br>**`lastSeen` is the feed position, not `firstSeen`.** A folded row moves *forward* when it recurs, so a cursor never steps over it and an ongoing outage is re-delivered with a higher count. Ordering by first occurrence would have been stable and wrong: a failure that started before your cursor and is still going would be reported once, ever. Two payload fields changed meaning in the same direction — `since` is where the record starts (**absent** when nothing was ever recorded, which is now genuinely "nothing has failed"), and `dropped` is now "could not be written down", the only remaining way an incident is lost.
  <br>**The invariant the merge turns on: an incident may repeat, a change may never be lost.** Two streams paged independently under one scalar cursor cannot both be exactly-once. The obvious move — return the *later* of the two positions — is wrong in the unacceptable direction, and it is not hypothetical: it made SH88's timestamp-tie test fail, because an incident minutes ahead of the audit page being walked advanced the cursor past rows the caller had never seen. So the cursor advances past an incident only when the change stream reports no `more`, meaning the audit has been drained to the ceiling and there is nothing for a later position to skip; until then the cursor stays the audit's and those incidents are simply read again, which costs nothing because rows are folded. There is now a test that pins exactly that.
  <br>**Shaped as its own array, not as a `Change` with an invented `action`.** Every existing caller branches on `action` and would have filed a failure as a content transition — pulling it into a file tree, counting it as work done. A separate array is a field a caller can ignore; a fake action is a field a caller can misread. Same reasoning in the terse rendering (`incident`, its own verb) and in `shio changes` (`!`-marked). Incidents carry **no site**, so a site-scoped read cannot narrow them and the `notes` say so rather than implying otherwise — no new visibility, since `/agent/diagnostics` has been instance-wide since SH103, and attributing them is filed as a follow-up. `shio report` picks them up for free: a webhook the front end never received is exactly a handoff concern, and it now appears in the handoff without a second call. Manifest: `durableIncidents`.

- **SH104** — **The handoff report** ([report.mjs](../cli/src/report.mjs), [commands/report.mjs](../cli/src/commands/report.mjs), `shio report`). Block K removed the human round trip that existed because the agent could not check its own work; this is the other half of the same brief — the one that exists because a human cannot see what the agent *did*. `shio verify` is the agent's output for a machine. This is its output for a person: what changed, a preview link per page, and the questions the CMS cannot settle itself, as Markdown ready for a PR body. 17 network-free tests ([report.test.mjs](../cli/test/report.test.mjs)).
  <br>**It composes three reads and adds no endpoint.** The SH88 feed knows what moved, the SH77 context pack knows each site's public URL, and the SH99 report knows what is unresolved — a `GET /agent/report` would be a fourth contract restating three (P10), and it would put *presentation* on the server, where a Markdown template then has to be versioned alongside the protocol. The pack is fetched as `include=sites` only: one field is needed from nine sections, and a read that pays for the other eight is a token bill nobody asked for (P3). **No MCP tool either** — the artifact's consumer is a human, so per-turn schema would be paid for something the agent hands to someone else, and the agent has a shell (the argument SH114's memory already made).
  <br>**Four rules, all of them about what a summary must not quietly omit.** A **deletion is a first-class row**: it has no address and no link, which makes it the row an implementation that builds the list out of links drops, and the row a reviewer most needs. A **preview link is never invented** — it exists when the site has a URL *and* the post has a friendly URL, and otherwise the report names which half is missing, because a plausible link that 404s costs the reader their trust in the whole document. The **warnings are the open questions** and errors are only *counted*, with the count in the first paragraph: an error is broken and belongs in the agent's loop before a human is asked to look, and restating each one here would create a second copy of the lint report that drifts from the first. And everything that makes the document less than complete — the feed's `more`, its lag note, a truncated or `partial` verify — goes in a **"What this report does not cover"** section *above* the footer, because this is the SH138 hazard at its worst: a shortened list of changes reads exactly like a complete review of a small change set, and the document exists to be trusted *instead of* the diff.
  <br>**A read does not move a cursor.** The report waited on SH88 so it could start where the last one ended, but advancing the position as a side effect of reading means running it twice gives two answers and the second says "nothing changed" — which for a review artifact reads as approval. So `--since last` reads a position and only **`--mark`** writes one, and `--mark` **refuses** when the report carried caveats about its own completeness: a cursor moved past changes nobody saw is a permanent hole in the review trail. That is the same refusal `pull --content` makes about a truncated projection. Losing the context pack degrades to naming why each link is absent rather than to failing — the failure must cost the links, not the document.

**Follow-up — the route proof that closes the warning**

- **SH141** — **Proving a route from the delivery side** ([ShAgentDeliveryProbe](../shio-app/src/main/java/com/viglet/shio/api/agent/verify/ShAgentDeliveryProbe.java), [ShFrontEndRoutes](../shio-app/src/main/java/com/viglet/shio/api/agent/verify/ShFrontEndRoutes.java), the `delivery` group on [ShAgentCheck](../shio-app/src/main/java/com/viglet/shio/api/agent/verify/ShAgentCheck.java) + [ShAgentVerifyService](../shio-app/src/main/java/com/viglet/shio/api/agent/verify/ShAgentVerifyService.java), `shio verify --delivery`). SH100 answered "internal links resolve" against the content graph, which was the right first move — no front end, no network, runs in a cold CI checkout — and could not see the failure §IX names as the most common one: **a page that exists in the CMS and 404s on the site**. So `link-unresolved` was a warning, because a warning is what you emit when you are not sure. This makes it sure: each published page and each unresolved link is requested from the site's own origin, and a non-2xx becomes `route-not-served` or `link-broken`, both **errors**. 15 tests ([ShAgentDeliveryTest](../shio-app/src/test/java/com/viglet/shio/api/agent/verify/ShAgentDeliveryTest.java) runs a real loopback front end — a mocked fetch cannot reproduce a *disagreement between two systems*, it only fails however the mock was written; [ShFrontEndRoutesTest](../shio-app/src/test/java/com/viglet/shio/api/agent/verify/ShFrontEndRoutesTest.java)).
  <br>**It is not a crawler, and the difference is the design.** It follows no link it did not already know about and visits each URL once, so the pass is bounded by the *content* rather than by the site's shape. SH101 had already built the one thing needed — an origin-checked, operator-consented fetch — and the extraction into `ShAgentDeliveryProbe` is the point: two callers of a security-relevant guard is one caller too many for a private method, since the second copy is where the origin check eventually goes missing. The render digest now shares the client too, which also fixes a wart it never noticed — it built an `HttpClient` (and its selector thread, and a cold connection pool) per call.
  <br>**The exception is declared, never guessed.** A front end legitimately owns routes the CMS has never heard of, so the answer had to be *declared*, and the store whose whole purpose is "facts about this instance that are not content" already exists: a **SH114 memory note keyed `frontend-routes`**, globs (`*` inside a segment, `**` across), scoped to a site or instance-wide, attributed, carried in the context pack, surviving a prune, one `shio remember` away. And the rule that keeps it honest: **a declaration silences a guess but never a proof** — with fetching off the link is not reported, and with the delivery pass on it is still fetched, so a declared route the site 404s is an error, because the declaration made a claim and the claim is checkable. Suppression that survives contact with evidence is how a baseline rots into a blanket, which is the hazard SH142 was careful about. A pattern that is not a path is dropped rather than compiled — here the dangerous failure mode is the one that matches *everything*, and it would be silent.
  <br>**Not in the default set unless an operator asked for it.** `ShAgentCheck`'s law is that every group defaults to on, and this is an application of it rather than an exception: the group is in the defaults exactly when `shio.agent.render.allow-fetch` is set, because on every other instance it cannot run at all and including it would fail a report on the absence of a deployment. Naming it while fetching is off is a teaching **400** (`delivery-disabled`), for the reason SH143 refuses an unresolvable `folder=`: a check that silently covered nothing while answering `ok` is the worst false green there is. The same distinction settles "no site has a URL" — a **400** when the caller named the group, a per-site **warning** when it arrived by default, since a group that joined on its own must not fail a call that never asked.
  <br>**Three bounds, and every cut is visible.** `max-fetches` (50) bounds the count, `fetch-budget-millis` (15s) bounds the *time* — not the same bound, since fifty pages behind a slow front end is four minutes, which is not a verification call but a hang — and an unreachable origin ends that site's pass after **one** request, reporting **one** `delivery-unreachable`: fifty copies of "it is down" is a report nobody reads, and the site's other pages are *unknowable*, not broken. Everything skipped goes in `notes`, and `shio verify` now prints `notes` at all — they were invisible in that output until this needed them, which had been quietly costing SH143's truncated-feed note too.
  <br>**`routes` hands the unresolved links over instead of warning about them.** The two rules answer the same question, and a defect reported once as a maybe and once as a fact is a report the reader has to de-duplicate. Manifest: `deliveryProof`, reported separately from `renderFetch` even though one property governs both, because an agent reading only the latter would never learn that `link-unresolved` can be an error here. **Deliberately not on the MCP tool schema:** a tool description is re-sent every turn (P3), and on the instances where this is `false` it would be a tax for a capability that cannot run — the manifest is the discovery surface, and `shio_verify`'s `checks` argument passes the group through unchanged. Tool-list budget: unmoved.

**Follow-ups — verification for a page made of sections**

- **SH154** — **The lint sees a section reference** ([ShPostReferenceFields](../shio-app/src/main/java/com/viglet/shio/api/agent/verify/ShPostReferenceFields.java), [ShAgentVerifyService](../shio-app/src/main/java/com/viglet/shio/api/agent/verify/ShAgentVerifyService.java)) and **SH169** — **the render digest composes the way the page does** ([ShAgentRenderService](../shio-app/src/main/java/com/viglet/shio/api/agent/verify/ShAgentRenderService.java)). Two shipped features, each correct alone, both blind to the pattern SH95 introduced: the `dangling-reference` rule knew a reference held as an **id** (`Content Select`, `File`) and not one held as a **friendly URL**, and the digest reads a post's own markup — which a section page has none of. So a page could name a section that did not exist and `verify` answered `ok`, and home, pricing and a genuinely blank page all hashed to `e3b0c442…`, the hash of nothing. The digest could answer neither question it exists for.
  <br>**One mechanism serves both, and picking it was most of the work.** A `Multi Select` is a free-form list of strings by design and most of them are tags, so neither reader could just treat values as URLs — that rule would report a defect for every tag on every post. The field now *declares* what it holds, in the model, which is the one place both readers already look: `widgetSettings: {"multiselect":{"references":"post"}}`. A **new key** rather than overloading the existing `multiselect.postType`, because that one says *which* type and a page's sections are deliberately heterogeneous — overloading it would mean naming one type and lying. A convention ("a field called `sections`") was the alternative and is unenforceable: nothing can check prose. The `@viglet/shio-model` DSL carries it (`references: "post"`), `@viglet/shio-sections` declares it on `Page`, and `pnpm -C shio-sections run emit` regenerated the two packages that ship it.
  <br>**The lint keeps both properties of the id-shaped rule:** an unpublished target on a published page stays the existing `unpublished-dependency` case — same failure, different spelling — and a target this credential cannot read is re-checked against the repository rather than reported as dangling, so the SH2 allow-list never manufactures a defect. A value that names a post of the wrong type (when `postType` narrows it) is its own `wrong-reference-type` finding.
  <br>**The digest reads the model, not a list of the eight first-party types.** A section's structure is not in one HTML field: the vocabulary's components render its title as a heading and its text fields as prose. So the mapping is stated once in terms of what the model says about a field — a title field becomes a heading, a markup field contributes its parsed structure, any other text field contributes its words — and it runs the *same parser*, so there is one notion of "structure" rather than a second path that would drift. A digest that knew the shipped section types by name would stop working the first time somebody wrote a ninth.
  <br>**An unresolvable section is marked, not skipped.** Contributing nothing is the original failure wearing a different hat: two different mistakes would hash the same. It contributes a heading naming the gap, so the digest moves when a reference breaks. The cost is real and stated: a page digest now reads N+1 posts, which is the same scoping pressure as **SH143**.

It never averages: a green from three and a red from one is a red, named on the subject; an instrument that did not run is unproven and never green, printed with what it would have answered; and an instrument only disagrees about a subject it covered, so silence from a run that never looked at a page cannot invent one. The two vocabularies normalise to the served path, home page included. It composes rather than forks (P10) — each instrument is its own command's `run` with a captured stdout — and `audit`/`snapshot` are opt-in and bounded with the bound declared, because choosing a baseline for the caller would invent the thing whose absence is the question.
- **SH610** — The seven repeated headings are merged: each block keeps one heading, the follow-up regions moved inside it in the order the file already had, and their titles are bold paragraphs because a region ends at the next heading of any level. cli/test/changelog-blocks.test.mjs is the obligation the lint never had - it matches a block label at any heading level, which is what makes it see the seven a heading-level-two regex reports none of.
- **SH594** — cli/test/known-debt.test.mjs reads all four ledgers through one LEDGERS table and answers what none of them can - what this repository is knowingly carrying, and which of it has an owner who has already gone. It does not merge the files, whose scopes differ; a fifth is one row. It landed red on the case its own rationale predicted, an open-findings entry owned by SH555 after SH555 shipped, re-filed as SH606.
- **SH204** — An incident carries its site where one is knowable, and `site=` narrows the feed's incident array the way it narrows its changes. Four of the six recorders attribute a failure now — the webhook dispatcher from the event it is delivering (free, already captured), both render paths from the page's own site, the Turing listener from the published post, and the SH15 sweep from a finder that returns the site beside the id rather than querying inside a catch. `api-error` and `transform` cannot ever, so an absent site means instance-level rather than unrecorded. The site is in the fold key, without which one webhook URL two sites subscribe folds into one row claiming whichever failed first; the scoping rule is the audit trail's exactly, since one cursor walks both streams; and `ShAgentIncidentLog.record` collapsed to one six-argument method because a five-argument `siteId` overload and the five-argument `frames` one are the same signature. Asserted by `ShAgentIncidentSiteTest`.
- **SH205** — An incident's identity is a `signature` — the message with runs of digits collapsed — and the message itself is overwritten with the most recent occurrence. Folding was keyed on prose written for a human, so "gave up after 3 attempt(s), last status 500" and the same webhook's 503 next publish were two rows: it failed on a flapping target, the highest-volume case and the one whose every occurrence differs, and the near-duplicates evicted unrelated incidents through the cap while looking exactly like several real problems. Digits cover every varying part of every message here, including inside exception text nobody could enumerate, and the standing objection that over-folding hides a failure is answered by the split rather than ignored: a wrong fold is one row carrying the newest text. Case is kept, and a collision must survive an identical kind, subject and site. Existing rows are backfilled with their own message so they age out rather than merging into rows a reader has already seen as separate. Asserted by `ShAgentIncidentSignatureTest`.
- **SH206** — `verify()` is three phases — read, fetch, assemble — and the read-only transaction spans only the first, so the SH141 network pass no longer holds a pooled connection while a front end is slow. It is a `TransactionTemplate` rather than the two beans §IX.7 proposed: an annotation cannot end a transaction mid-method, which is what forced the bean split, and a programmatic boundary sidesteps the proxy without cutting the block's largest class in half. It also fixes the case a bean split would have missed — `ShAgentProofService` calls verify from inside its own transaction, so on that path the fetches were never in a transaction this class opened. The read pass returns a `Plan` holding no entity, because `Scan` is full of rows that detach at commit. `delivery` became a gather returning plain Strings; `report` and `deliveryCoverage` take a `siteNames` map, which also removed `siteById` and with it a full site-table read per finding. The bounds stay, for the reason the design asked. Asserted by `ShAgentVerifyTransactionTest` on the calling thread, since a loopback handler's thread would have reported no transaction either way; `ShRenderCacheReachLintTest` learned to read code rather than prose and to see a programmatic boundary at all.
- **SH207** — The console navigation carries an indicator of how many agent runs are awaiting a decision, absent at zero, opening the SH109 review queue. §IX.8 settled the position before the content and it held: a banner on every page is noise and a banner on the review page is a page nobody visits, so what shipped is an unread-shaped count. `GET /api/v2/review/pending` is its own read because `/sessions` scans 2000 audit rows and resolves each post one at a time - fine for a page somebody opened, not for every console render - and this one is two queries. It counts runs, matching the list it opens, since a badge whose number appears nowhere on the page it links to is one nobody can reconcile. A `ReviewPendingProvider` holds it so the queue can invalidate it after an approve. The count is deliberately not `ShReviewSession.pending`: that counts audit entries and, because publish keeps the DRAFT row as the editable copy, never decreases - filed as SH615. This read asks the question that makes an indicator usable instead: a draft with no published twin, or one modified after its twin was published, so approving takes it to zero. Asserted by `ShReviewPendingTest`, whose fixture is rebuilt per test because approve is one of the things under test.
- **SH208** — Every `HELP` is now `helpText("<command>")` reading `cli/src/help/<command>.txt` — thirty texts moved out of JavaScript into files with no syntax to get wrong. The class is removed rather than managed: prose about a CLI names commands, command names attract backticks, and a backtick inside a template literal is a syntax error that stops the whole binary loading. It happened three times in three sessions and only the three tests that spawn the CLI ever noticed, because every other CLI test imports the command modules directly. §IX.9's other candidate does not work and the lint says so in an assertion: `String.raw` changes how backslash escapes are read and has no effect on the delimiter, so a backtick still ends the literal — a fix that would have looked right and removed nothing. SH377's pair case is the reason an escape rule was not enough either: two backticks parse fine and silently truncate the help, measured at 149 lines instead of 200 with `Common options` gone. `help-source.test.mjs` refuses the next template-literal `HELP` and checks every `helpText(...)` has a file behind it; the SH377 guard in `index.test.mjs` kept its end-to-end half, since "the output reaches its last line" never depended on the cause. Commands are imported lazily, so one run reads one file. `files: ["src"]` already ships them.
- **SH616** — The single-page path now unwraps the capture before writing it. SH526 made `capture` return `{bytes, shape}`, and `--against` was taught to unwrap it while this path kept passing the whole object to `writeFile` — so `shio snapshot <page>`, the command's original purpose, could not write a PNG at all. Nothing was red because every fixture drives `ctx.capture`, which hands back a bare Buffer: a seam that differs from production in *shape* rather than in behaviour, which is the one kind of double that can be green about something that cannot work. Found while SH209 was reworking the same function, and closed with a fixture that returns the production envelope and a `writeFile` that refuses anything but bytes, the way the real one does.
- **SH209** — `shio snapshot --site <name>` photographs every published page, one baseline each, and reports which moved. The parts existed - `/agent/find` gives the addresses and `capture` takes the picture - so what this adds is the loop's own three properties. One browser for the sweep, which `withBrowser` now owns: `capture` used to launch and close one per photograph, so even a one-page `--against` at two widths launched four, and over a site that is the difference between a run and a wait. A per-page timeout, so one page that never settles cannot consume the run. And an unreachable page is never an unchanged one - SH141's lesson arriving in a second place: a page the browser could not open is named with its reason, is never scored, and exits 1 on its own, independently of `--fail-on-change`, because a visual change is usually intended and a page nobody could open is not a change at all. A failure is caught per page, so the sweep does not end at the first bad one, which is the failure mode a set exists to remove. Drafts are skipped rather than previewed: photographing the preview would silently answer a different question, and `--preview` is how a caller asks for that. A page and `--site` together are refused rather than resolved by precedence. Asserted by six cases in `snapshot.test.mjs`, whose fixture returns the production capture envelope rather than a bare Buffer - which is how SH616 was found.
- **SH617** — The backtick half of `help.test.mjs`'s SH435 guard is retired. It asserted that no command's help contained a raw backtick, because a backtick ends a template literal - a lone one broke the parse, a pair silently truncated the text. Both were properties of the help being JavaScript, and SH208 made it a `.txt`, where a backtick is a character. So the rule had stopped protecting anything and started taxing the one thing help about a CLI most wants to do, which is quote a command name. It surfaced the ordinary way: the next command written after SH208 went red for prose that could not hurt anyone. The interpolation half is kept and re-stated on its own terms - a flat file prints `${…}` verbatim, and a placeholder nobody filled in reads as output - while `help-source.test.mjs` owns the mechanism by refusing the literal itself. Recorded rather than folded into SH208, which had already shipped: a guard that outlives its mechanism is its own kind of defect, and the interesting part is that removing a failure mode leaves a guard behind that nothing then re-reads.
- **SH397** — `shio doctor` answers "can I work here" in one call: the instance and which build, the credentials, SH295's render-model drift, the sites, and whether a local content tree exists. Every fact already had a reader and none had a caller, so the first minutes of a session were five calls and a guess. Three outcomes rather than two - `ok`, `FAIL`, and `??` for a fact that could not be established - because an instance that does not answer leaves four checks unanswerable, and reporting those as failures would invent four defects out of one: SH141's rule for a page it could not fetch, and SH209's for one it could not photograph, arriving in a third place. Exit 1 on a `FAIL` only, since running it with no instance is how somebody checks their own tree. The design's first half was already shipped by SH460 and is what this reads: `version` says `dev` on any instance not run from a packaged jar - the same string before and after a rebuild - and `builtAt`, stamped from the newest class the JVM loaded, is the comparable fact. Its absence is now reported rather than left to read as current, which is the whole defect. It deliberately does not run `push --content --check`: that needs the server, a projection and a plan, inside a command whose promise is one quick answer, so it reports that a tree exists and names the expensive check as the next thing to run. Asserted by eight cases in `doctor.test.mjs`.
- **SH423** — `ShContextCacheHeadroomTest` carries a declared count, asserted exactly, so spending a slot is a diff somebody reviews rather than a number that moves - in both directions, since a task that frees one and does not lower it hands the next task a budget it will spend believing it was always there. The headroom prints on every run, which is what turns a wall into a gauge: SH347 reported arrival and this reports approach. The measurement came first and changed the task. The counter counted distinct `jdbc:h2:mem:` URLs, and Spring keys on the whole MergedContextConfiguration - so two classes on one URL with different properties are two contexts, read as one. It said 56 where the suite creates 62, a systematic undercount the margin of 8 was silently absorbing rather than a lower bound anybody could act on. The counter now reads `properties`, `@Import`, `webEnvironment` and `@DynamicPropertySource`, measured to be the closed set because no test uses `@TestPropertySource`, `@ContextConfiguration`, `@ActiveProfiles` or `@MockitoBean`; `*IT.java` is excluded because failsafe runs in its own JVM; and the file excludes itself, since its own guard-the-guard literals added a phantom context and a phantom database the moment they were written. The margin is 2, covering only the four classes whose properties are registered at runtime. The honest state is 62 of 64 with zero spare, so the next context is a decision about the ceiling instead of a surprise. The second half of the design - a shared context with per-test site scoping - is untouched and now has a truthful number to be judged against.
- **SH618** — `shio diff --against proposal` is the second link of SH522's chain. `--against capture` asks what a reader gets; this asks whether the write did what the plan said - the accepted blocks became sections carrying the fields they promised, and each page composes the ones it was supposed to. Both sides are declarations, so it is a set difference rather than a scan, it needs no capture, and the branch is taken before the inventory is read. Keeping the two questions apart is the design: a page that composes the right sections and serves them badly is the capture's finding, and merging them would leave a reader unable to tell "the conversion did not do what it promised" from "it did, and the layout is wrong". Four outcomes per row - ok, absent (declared, never made), incomplete (made, missing a promised field, the shape the 106-field hand-count got wrong) and undeclared (the plan accepts a block the proposal never had, which is two declarations disagreeing before the artefact is involved). A gained field is reported and never a failure, the rule a gained link already had. SH522 stays open for the document and an earlier moment, and its refusal now names those two and no longer names the proposal - the half a shrinking allow-list usually gets wrong, since it would send a reader away from a verb they have. Seven assertions in `cli/test/diff-proposal.test.mjs`.
- **SH528** — The fixture carries the traits that broke real replicas, each named with the task that needed it: a query string on an asset path, a `./../../` reference served four segments deeper than its source (SH512), a fixed overlay first in the markup (SH505), a `&` escaped twice (SH476/SH565), a zero-byte file behind a 200 and an image content-type (SH514), a `<canvas>` a script creates so a plain fetch and `--render` disagree (SH517), a page under a locale prefix, and a link that is wrong. Both fixtures gained them - the socket one the conformance suite serves and the injected-fetch twin - because their shared header claimed the two differ only in where the bytes come from and nothing enforced it; `fixture-traits.test.mjs` now does. They sit at depth 2 behind `/about` with a stylesheet of their own, so a `--depth 1` run meets none of them and every existing count, asset list and theme is untouched. One entry pins a defect rather than its cure: the double-escaped title arrives whole, which is SH565 still open and now reproducible with no network - asserting the repair would make the catalogue fail for the thing it exists to preserve. Running the conformance gate was what made this safe: `pnpm test` was green while the suite's own `unfollowed` assertion, the twin of one already updated, was still red. It needed `SHIO_CONFORMANCE_ALLOW_STALE=1`, because a fat-jar instance reports `commit` matching HEAD and a null `builtAt` - SH609, reproduced live, and its refusal claims "no build identity at all" while the commit is right there.
- **SH620** — `src/main/resources/ui/` is empty of tracked files now. SH21's commit subject is "delete legacy AngularJS resources/ui tree" and it left `shio.js`, `shio.min.js`, `shFeature.js` and `shSystem.js` behind - about 456 KB that nothing referenced and nothing served, since Spring Boot serves `resources/public/**` and `resources/static/**` and never `resources/ui/**`. Dead weight in every release since Block E. Nobody saw it because a deletion of 330 files is reviewed by its diff, and a diff shows what went rather than what stayed. Found by writing SH529's assertion for that debt entry rather than by looking: the entry claimed the removal was unasserted, and the assertion came back red. `ShRemovalsStayedRemovedTest` now holds all three of the block's removals - the AngularJS bundles by name, the Thymeleaf starter, and SH60's four deprecated widget names - keyed on file names rather than on the directory, so a working copy carrying untracked leftovers is a local state and not a failing build.
- **SH529** — The debt list carries a verdict per group, which is what SH527 left open: it established the count and held it as a named list, and the question "which of these earn an assertion" went unanswered. Every group now reads EARNS or DOES NOT, with the shape the assertion would take, ordered by whether the defect could return rather than by cost - which inverts the obvious order. A removal is the cheapest entry on the list and ranks first, because an absence has nobody looking at it; the sixteen console entries rank last despite being the largest group, because a broken editor page is seen the first time somebody opens the console. One entry earns a reader rather than an assertion: SH238 is asserted in `shio-react/e2e`, a tree the reader does not walk because it needs a running instance, and a second assertion would duplicate a passing one - listed rather than exempted, because an exemption would claim it cannot be asserted when it is asserted and merely unread. The first group is paid: `ShRemovalsStayedRemovedTest` closes SH20, SH21 and SH60, and the debt fell from 43 to 40. Writing it found SH620 - SH21 had never finished, leaving four tracked files of the legacy AngularJS bundle in `src/main/resources/ui/` under a commit that says it deleted the tree, shipping in every jar for two blocks. That is the argument for the exercise in one case: the entry said unasserted, and the assertion came back red.
- **SH561** — The corpus run has a second driver that speaks the transport: `mcp-transport.conformance.mjs` spawns `shio mcp` and issues newline-delimited JSON-RPC, asserting initialize, every tool's name and object input schema, the `tools/list` budget, a real `tools/call`, a refusal, and an unknown tool name. The client is hand-rolled for `fixture-site.mjs`'s reason - an SDK that knows the protocol would paper over the framing this exists to check - and it reads stdout only, because the bridge's status line goes to stderr and that channel separation is part of the contract rather than a detail. Two things it measured on its first run. `tools/list` has two tokens of headroom, ~2373 against 2375, over the wire, which no module call ever serialises. And the budget has to be measured on `result.tools`, the subject `ShMcpToolBudgetTest` names: counting the whole `result` read 2376 and reported a one-token regression that was this file counting the envelope - two instruments for one budget must agree on the subject or the second is noise with a stack trace. One thing the design assumed is not so: the replication chain has no MCP tool, since `clone`, `propose` and `convert` are a CLI path and the eleven tools are the content surface, so "the same chain over tools/call" is not a scenario that exists and saying so is more useful than inventing one. The design's "thirteen tools" is stale prose - there are eleven, and three files in the tools package are not tools. The module driver stays: faster, and it localises a failure. What it cannot be is evidence about the wire.
- **SH562** — `ShConvertedLayoutRenderTest` renders the vocabulary page and asserts every `shio-` class on an annotated element is one the generated theme defines, reading `VOCABULARY_THEME_CSS` out of `cli/src/vocabulary-theme.mjs` - the same cross-language read the class already does for `convert.mjs`, for SH245's reason. Half the task was already shipped and worth saying so: SH555's escaped stylesheet got its Java assertion when SH555 itself landed, with a fixture carrying an `@font-face` precisely because the earlier sentinel had no quote, ampersand or angle bracket and survived escaping unchanged. What had no assertion on this side was SH556. It shipped an instrument in `convert.test.mjs`, which reads the declared union against the declared templates - two declarations agreeing with each other, and neither of them renders, so a template drawing a class the union forgot would still pass. This asserts the third thing: what a rendered page actually carries. Scoped to elements with a `data-shio-` handle on purpose, because a converted page also carries the source's own classes on markup it kept verbatim (SH575) and a check demanding the theme style those would fail on every working replica. Verified red by removing one rule from the theme, which named `shio-heading` and nothing else. It went into the existing class rather than a new one: that class already holds an isolated context, and the SH423 gauge is at 62 of 64 with no spare, so a new `@SpringBootTest` would have cost the slot this needed no part of.
- **SH563** — buildInventory now copies visit's redirectedTo onto the page row, so a path reached through a 301 is stored as one and the source's canonical choice survives the capture; SH560's redirect-recorded assertion goes green and its open-findings entry is deleted.
- **SH564** — propose stores an href that points back into the capture as the source-relative path, the way SH461's rewritten CSS already stores one, and leaves a genuinely external one whole. Internal is decided by the crawl origin OR by the capture holding that path - the awkward archetype declares one base and is served from another, so a same-host rule passes every unit test and leaves its ctaHref absolute. Only absolute references are touched: resolving a fragment made #top into /#top.
- **SH565** — scanPage decodes the title as it captures it, which is the seam SH476 and SH550 both routed around: a title is RCDATA, and one decodes text becoming a field while the other decodes attribute values and states raw-text bodies are excluded. It reached further than either - the title does not travel through propose, so fidelity was wrong too - and it compounded on re-capture. Decoded once, so a deliberately doubled entity keeps the distinction its author drew.
- **SH567** — The reader already walked shio-site/scripts, so what was left was the task's second half: re-judge the ten. Three of the copy group are now asserted beside the scripts that own them - the generated token figures, the prerender's route parity and the Markdown twin - taking the debt from 39 to 36. Two came off as false payments first: a comment naming an id, and a test filed under SH537 that asserted SH532's claim. And shio-site's test script named its files by hand, so the new one was scanned and never run.
- **SH569** — A sixth archetype whose every route answers badly - a dead internal link, a 500, a redirect loop, a linked JSON document, HTML served as text/plain and an oversized asset - and the corpus now asserts SH431's distinction: a data row and a problems row are different claims, because collapsing them makes the coverage gate read a bounded sample as complete. It found a real defect on its first run: the redirect follow said one hop and had no counter, so the loop route spun until the process died.
- **SH570** — A seventh archetype serving a 200 whose body is wrong - an unclosed block, no title, SH544's 265-character title, a nested form, a base href that disagrees with the serving path, and UTF-8 bytes under an iso-8859-1 header. Separate from SH569 because a scanner cannot report what a fetch already refused. The encoding assertion compares the stored title with the source file's bytes, never with what a terminal prints, and was verified to fail when pointed at the wrong file.
- **SH602** — Every teaching refusal is counted where they all already pass - one method in the controller advice - keyed by what was asked for rather than by what broke, and diagnostics reports the top ten. A didYouMean that fired is a separate kind from one that did not, because a near-miss is a naming problem and a name with no neighbour is a missing capability. Bounded at 200 distinct names with the drop count reported, since a counter that silently stops reads like a quiet instance.
- **SH603** — A second task shape driven end to end and scored with SH597's metric: build a small site from an empty instance, no capture and no corpus. Measured 5 calls and 1053 tokens, against 950 to 3650 for a single discovery intent - so the shape nothing was tuned for is not more expensive, which is the answer the task wanted. The first reading was 941 and measured nothing: three calls had failed, and the status guard that catches it is why the recorded figure is honest.
- **SH609** — builtAt resolves under java -jar: a Boot CodeSource is a nested jar URL that Paths.get refuses, so the field was null on precisely the deployment the conformance gate insists on - and SH500's dirty-tree fallback had nothing to fall back to, which made ALLOW_STALE the standing incantation. Everything before the first !/ is the outer jar and its lastModifiedTime is when the artifact was produced. Asserted from a fat-jar CodeSource so the null cannot return when packaging changes.
- **SH612** — Two recorders wrote past AFTER_COMMIT from a pool thread that never had a tenant bound, so the row was stamped with the default discriminator - and SH204's site id turned a merely invisible row into one carrying an identifier its own tenant cannot resolve. The tenant now crosses the boundary the way siteId and what already do: captured on the committing thread, restored around the write, and the far thread put back as it was found because a pool reuses it. The instrument is the deliverable (SH338): ShOffThreadTenantLintTest classifies every thread boundary in shio-app and found a third, larger one - SH639.
- **SH613** — A textual lint reads prose, so writing about a rule could fail the build for breaking it. The population was 20 tests that read Java source and five private comment-strippers with five ideas of what a comment is - ShSourceText is now the one, and @ShSourceScan makes each scan declare CODE, PROSE or BOTH, held to using the stripper or to a written reason. Ten of the twenty were reading prose by accident; four of those were counted by ShContextCacheHeadroomTest, which had noticed the hazard for itself and excluded itself rather than asking whether anybody else was affected - so the Spring context budget was reported as two slots more spent than it is.
- **SH635** — The unreproducible red was a scoping defect: readable(...) appended every site-less post in the instance to every scope, so a run that named a site was handed an error about a post in no site of theirs with a fix they cannot carry out. It is the rule folders(...) states one method away and posts never got. It read as a flake because whether the blueprint site verified clean depended on whether another class sharing the context had left an orphan behind - which depends on suite order, and SH613's new classes made it deterministic. The permanent capture this task shipped earlier is what named it on the first red run.
- **SH615** — The queue's per-run count asked whether the post has a DRAFT row, and publish keeps the draft as the editable copy - so every post that has ever existed has one and the number could only go up. A curator approved a run, the page reloaded with the same 'N to review', and Approve stayed enabled on published work. SH207 had already written the right definition one method away (unreleased: no published twin, or modified after it). Both halves landed together because the count also counted entries rather than posts, and a number that is fresh and still not a count of decisions reads as correct.
- **SH619** — read?state=published is the decision: a parameter on the read surface rather than a diff endpoint, so 'what will change when I publish this' composes out of two reads of one address instead of becoming a third contract (P10). A state naming a row the post has not got is a 404 that says which, never a fallback to the draft-preferred row - the fallback would hand a caller comparing draft against live the draft twice and read as 'nothing changed'. Landed on MCP as well as REST, and the tool description was trimmed 186 to 172 before the tools/list budget moved by the remaining 8.
- 🗑 **SH641** — superseded by SH630: A duplicate filed one commit earlier because SH630 was misread as shipped; its one distinct argument - that an assertion message IS a string literal, so stripping comments alone would be wrong - is carried into SH630, where the measurement showed both rules give the identical answer.
- **SH630** — The walk matched task ids over raw text, so a comment and an assertion message were the same bytes - and the failure only ever RETIRED debt, silently, at the moment somebody wrote carefully about why a task mattered. The count decided the rule: not-on-a-comment-line and inside-a-string-literal give the identical answer (428 of 524), so the parse buys nothing and the marker convention is unnecessary. 96 ids were being paid by prose; 88 shipped ones are now held in REVEALED, apart from the triaged DEBT, as SH642. Three scanners were quietly wrong while writing this - a regex literal desynced a comment stripper, and the fence check contained a fence - which is why the final rule holds no cross-line state outside Java.
- **SH639** — The sweep is a timer, so it ran with no tenant bound and Hibernate appended the default discriminator to finders over ShPostUnified: another tenant's due post was not published late, it was never found, with nothing thrown and nothing logged. SH612's capture had nothing to capture here, so the sweep iterates instead - one pass per non-suspended tenant, through runAs so the reused timer thread is left as it was found. A suspended tenant is skipped because publishing for an account the platform stopped is worse than publishing late; the tenant list is read once, so one provisioned mid-sweep waits for the next tick; and each pass is caught alone so one tenant's failure cannot silence the rest.
- **SH640** — The fourth SH522 declaration is built, and the three questions the read left open are answered in the comparison rather than in prose. Rich text compares VERBATIM - publishing copies the value across, so any difference is one a curator made, and a normalising comparison would hide a whitespace edit the CDA then serves differently (a semantic HTML diff is also the first step toward an instance that runs a browser). A missing field and an empty one are different findings, because deleting a value and never declaring the field are different acts. The answer is per site listed per post, because the question is asked before a batch. Only posts find already reported as live are read twice.
- **SH642** — The triage did not produce the expected verdicts. Every one of the 88 is already named by a suite file and 63 within a dozen lines of an assertion - none is silent, none is named only in source - so the verdict for the population is neither EARNS nor DOES NOT: the test exists and does not carry the id where the reader can see it. That is a different debt from the original 35, which have nothing standing behind them, and one figure mispriced both. REVEALED is now a map from id to the file that names it, which is the verdict and the payment instruction at once, split into the 63 that are a one-line move and the 25 named in a class docstring.
- **SH169** — The render digest hashed every section page to the hash of nothing; /agent/render now composes each referenced section title and fields into the outline, in declared order.
- **SH882** — DRAWN is decided by looking for the stored value in the served page, and only that gates; a value carrying its own annotations is not an uncuratable field.
- **SH883** — A one-token value counts as drawn only where it is a whole text node or attribute value, so a coincidental character stops being evidence and the two real findings survive.
- **SH885** — The CLI reader asks SH872's rule too, so a key the post's own markup annotates counts as declared and an annotated replica reads 7 of 10 instead of 7 of 4.

## Block I — Content as files (SH74)

> The block removes the *second* human round trip: authoring over HTTP. Content projects
> to a git-diffable text tree, the tree syncs both ways, and the merge is three-way — so
> a human curating in the console and an agent writing files are both first-class writers
> rather than one overwriting the other.

- **SH88** — **Change feed with a cursor** (`GET /api/v2/agent/changes`, `shio changes`, `since=` on `shio_changes`). [ShAgentChangesService](../shio-app/src/main/java/com/viglet/shio/api/agent/ShAgentChangesService.java) + [ShAgentChanges](../shio-app/src/main/java/com/viglet/shio/api/agent/dto/ShAgentChanges.java) + [ShAgentChangeCursor](../shio-app/src/main/java/com/viglet/shio/api/agent/ShAgentChangeCursor.java), with keyset queries on `ShHistoryRepository`. **The cursor is `(instant, id)`, not a timestamp** — the reason SH83 shipped a window and refused to fake one: audit rows share timestamps (a batch of twelve writes commits inside one second, and on a MariaDB with second-precision columns inside one *value*), so a timestamp cursor either re-delivers a whole second or silently drops the entries that tie. A cursor with no `|<id>` part is a **teaching 400** rather than an interpretation, because the failure it would cause is invisible. **Both modes share one order** (oldest → newest), so the cursor is always the last row and a caller never has to know which mode it got; an empty read returns the position it was given, and an empty *window* returns a synthetic anchor (`<ceiling>|`), so a quiet instance still yields a place to stand. **The lag rule:** SH51 writes the audit row inside the writer's transaction, so its timestamp is assigned *before* the commit and a slow transaction can land an older timestamp behind a cursor that already passed it — the feed therefore refuses to report anything younger than `now - shio.agent.changes.lag-millis` (1s default). That narrows the window rather than closing it, and the response says so in `notes` instead of implying exactness; the real fix is **SH147**. **A leak closed on the way:** `shio_changes` read the whole trail through `findRecent`, ignoring the SH2 per-site allow-list, so a scoped token could see the titles of content it could not fetch — both surfaces now route through this service, which scopes to readable sites (and keeps unattributable rows for unrestricted credentials only). Rows carry an SH79 address, resolved once per object and absent when the object is gone (the normal state of a `DELETE` row, whose title travels in `what`). Flips the manifest's `changeCursor`, which was reported `false` through Blocks H and K on purpose. 11 tests ([ShAgentChangesTest](../shio-app/src/test/java/com/viglet/shio/api/agent/ShAgentChangesTest.java)). → was §X.3
- **SH86** — **The filesystem projection format** ([cli/src/content-files.mjs](../cli/src/content-files.mjs)): one post, one `shio/content/<site>/<url>.md` — YAML frontmatter for the metadata and fields, the post's rich-text field as the document body. Pure and unit-tested, in the shape `post-types-io.mjs` established. The four design questions the roadmap left open, answered: (1) **the path is the friendly URL, not the folder chain** — a URL is unique per site by definition so the tree cannot collide, and the folder travels in frontmatter because SH79 is explicit that the two are separate namespaces and deriving one from the other would place content in the wrong folder silently; (2) **only the DRAFT projects**, and `publish:` in a file is an *instruction* a push forwards rather than state a pull writes back (P7 — a tree holding both copies would make "what does the site show?" a question about which file you opened); (3) **`fields:` is nested** under its own key, because a post-type may legitimately have a field called `type` or `url` and a flat map would let content overwrite the document's identity; (4) **anything that is not a scalar or a list of scalars stays compact JSON** — a YAML rendering of arbitrary nesting is a second serialization format to specify and get wrong, and the write side already speaks JSON. **Losslessness is absolute, and the format gives up prettiness to keep it:** a value that would not survive the round trip (leading/trailing whitespace, an empty string, a body that is not exactly its own trim) stays in `fields:` as a JSON string instead of becoming the body, and the one normalization — a body's CRLF becomes LF — exists precisely so a pull cannot report a change nobody made. The body field is chosen as the first `HTML Editor` field by ordinal and **written into the file** as `body:`, so reading a projection back never consults the model; a `Text Area` is deliberately never promoted, since a rule that guessed at the "main" text field would move content between fields the moment someone added one. A hand-written file takes its `site`/`url` from its path (law P4: `Write` should not require ceremony), and a path that *disagrees* with the frontmatter is refused rather than guessed — a rename on one side only is a move on one side and a create on the other, which is SH134's lesson arriving on the file side. 13 tests ([content-files.test.mjs](../cli/test/content-files.test.mjs)). → was §X.1
- **SH87** — **Two-way content sync**: `shio pull --content` and `shio push --content` ([content-pull.mjs](../cli/src/commands/content-pull.mjs), [content-push.mjs](../cli/src/commands/content-push.mjs), [content-store.mjs](../cli/src/content-store.mjs)) — the same two verbs the model already had, over the other resource, so an agent that learned pull/push does not learn a second vocabulary for pages. Push compiles the tree into one desired-state document per site and applies it through `POST /agent/plan`/`/apply` (P10 — no third write path, so atomicity, teaching errors and prune rules are the ones already tested), which makes `--check` the content-tree drift guard beside `shio push --check` (SH65) and `shio apply --check` (SH129). Folders are declared from the posts' own `folder` values **plus every ancestor**, because a document declaring `/blog/2026` without `/blog` would put a whole level outside its own prune scope. **Two refusals worth naming, both of the same family as SH138:** a **truncated** `find` result means the projection would omit posts, and the very next `push --prune` would read those gaps as deletions — so pull refuses to write a partial projection unless `--allow-partial`, and the snapshot it then writes stays marked `partial` so a later prune refuses too (the cap itself is **SH146**); and `push --content` on an empty content directory is an error, because "no files" plus `--prune` is a request to delete a section and is far more often a wrong `--content-dir`. 13 command tests ([content-commands.test.mjs](../cli/test/content-commands.test.mjs)). → was §X.2
- **SH89** — **Conflict policy: a three-way merge, per field** ([content-sync.mjs](../cli/src/content-sync.mjs)). A sync with only "mine" and "theirs" has to pick one, and picking is a clobber; both actors here are legitimate writers, so the engine keeps the **base** — what the two sides last agreed on — in `shio/.shio/content-base.json` along with the SH88 cursor. One side changing takes that side; different fields changing on each side **merge**; the same field changing on both is a conflict named by field (`fields.headline`). **Metadata merges by the same rule**, so a post moved in the console and rewritten in a file is not a conflict. **No conflict markers, ever:** `<<<<<<<` in a field value is *content*, and the next push would send it to the server and the next publish would put it on the site — so a conflict writes nothing for that post, is reported with a non-zero exit, and `--show-remote` drops the server's copy beside the file as `<file>.remote` so a diff is still one command away; `--ours`/`--theirs` resolve deliberately. **The rule that makes push safe** is the one that is easy to get wrong: a post the tree did *not* change but the server *did* is declared with the **server's own values** — declaring the base would quietly revert a console edit, and omitting the post would drop it out of the declared set where `--prune` would delete it. A deletion on either side is never silently undone: server-deleted plus untouched file deletes the file, file-deleted plus untouched server stays deleted and waits for `--prune`, and deleted-on-one-side-edited-on-the-other is a conflict. 15 engine tests ([content-sync.test.mjs](../cli/test/content-sync.test.mjs)). → was §X.4
- **SH90** — **`shio dev --content`** ([content-watch.mjs](../cli/src/commands/content-watch.mjs)): a file watcher on the content tree plus a poll of the SH88 feed, both funnelling into one `syncOnce` that **pulls before it pushes** — bringing the server's edits down first is what makes a simultaneous edit *visible* instead of overwritten, and a conflict stops the push for that run rather than leaving the tree and the instance in a state neither side asked for. Bursts coalesce (one sync per burst, one rerun if a trigger arrives mid-run) and the loop returns a stoppable handle instead of blocking, which is also what lets it be tested with no clock. The record is **JSONL** at `shio/.shio/dev-events.jsonl` — one object per event with its kind, counts and timestamp — because a failure buried in a long scrollback costs the agent a reconstruction, while `grep` over one-object-per-line answers "did anything conflict while I was working?" directly. Human-readable lines still go to stdout; losing the log never stops the sync it describes. `shio dev` without `--content` is unchanged, and `--content` deliberately does *not* spawn the site's dev server (a content repo has no `run dev` script to spawn). → was §X.5
- **Block I wiring** — manifest: `contentAsFiles` and `changeCursor` both flip to `true` (each was `false` through two blocks so that flipping it would mean something), and `/agent/changes` joins the curated endpoint index. CLI: `shio changes` (`--since`, `--since last` reading the last pull's position, `--cursor` for `SINCE=$(shio changes --cursor)`, `--site`, `--limit`, `--json`) and `--content` on `pull`/`push`/`dev`. Terse rendering for the feed ([ShAgentChangesTerse](../shio-app/src/main/java/com/viglet/shio/api/agent/ShAgentChangesTerse.java)) puts the cursor on the **header** line, since it is the one value the caller must carry forward and burying it after fifty rows would end the cheapest read on the surface with a search. `shio_changes` gains `since` without adding a tool, so the SH132 tool-list budget is unchanged; the SH130 golden was regenerated and the diff is exactly the new parameter. **A pre-existing test fragility fixed rather than worked around:** `ShAgentContextTest`'s "budget that cuts the sitemap" was three quarters of the whole pack, but the mandatory sections are charged first and the **model is instance-wide**, so any new test class that adds a post-type pushed them past the cut and starved the sitemap of every row — the helper now measures the sitemap's own cost, so the cut lands where the test means it whatever else the shared database holds.

**Follow-up**

- **SH173** — **`push --content` no longer fails on content it does not manage** ([content-store.mjs](../cli/src/content-store.mjs), [content-push.mjs](../cli/src/commands/content-push.mjs), [format-error.mjs](../cli/src/format-error.mjs)). Without `--site` the push read the server side of the merge for *every* post on the instance, so one un-addressable post in an unrelated site took the whole command down — the CI gate failing on somebody else's data, with seven hundred characters of request URL and no `fix`. Three fixes, all three of which the design asked for:
  <br>**Scope is derived, not configured.** `shio/content/<site>/**` already names the sites a tree holds, so `sitesOf()` reads exactly those. `--site` existing was not a reason for the tool to need telling what its own directory says. A first pull into an empty tree still reads the instance, which is the one case where that is the intent.
  <br>**An unreadable post is a finding.** SH171's per-row errors turn what was a fatal 404 into a named list — "these N posts could not be read by address, run `shio verify`" — and the merge proceeds over the content that read fine.
  <br>**A remote failure prints the teaching body.** Shio always sends an SH80 problem; the CLI was printing `Shio CDA 404 for <url>` and discarding it. It now prints the title, detail, `at`, `didYouMean`, `allowed` and `fix`, and the URL moved behind `SHIO_DEBUG` — it is diagnostic detail, not the message. `formatError` is its own module because `index.mjs` runs the CLI on import, and a formatting test should not have to start the tool.
- **SH198** — **the CLI suite runs green, and the diagnosis was not what the symptom said** ([test/support/paths.mjs](../cli/test/support/paths.mjs), [verify-baseline.test.mjs](../cli/test/verify-baseline.test.mjs), [blueprints.test.mjs](../cli/test/blueprints.test.mjs), [init.test.mjs](../cli/test/init.test.mjs), [content-commands.test.mjs](../cli/test/content-commands.test.mjs), [package.json](../cli/package.json)). 199/199 in ~250 ms, exit 0, **with stdin open**. The roadmap recorded two independent problems measured twice a block apart — a hang blamed on a test reading stdin, and 7 failures across four areas — and both readings were wrong in the same way: they were one cause each, and the second was a *consequence* of the first triage never completing.
  <br>**The 7 failures were one mistake.** Every one was a fake filesystem keyed on the POSIX path literal its author typed, compared against what the command actually passes — `path.join`, which on Windows is `\repo\shio\verify-baseline.json`. The lookup misses, `readFile` throws `ENOENT`, the command takes its legitimate "no such file" branch, and the assertion that finally fails is about a *message* several steps downstream. Four files, four different symptoms, one line of cause. `content-commands.test.mjs` had the answer from the start — a local `norm()` — and the files added after it did not copy it, so `norm`/`endsWithPath` now live in `test/support/paths.mjs` with the reasoning attached. The commands were never wrong: they write to a real disk and must join like it.
  <br>**The hang was the 7th failure, not a companion to it.** `dev --content` arms a real `setInterval`, and its test called `handle.stop()` *after* the assertions — so the one that failed on `/shio\/content$/` (a Windows path again) skipped the cleanup, and the timer held the event loop open. `node --test` printed all 199 results and then sat there: the 600s CI timeout was spent entirely *after* the suite had finished. Nothing in the suite reads process stdin — every stdin test injects `ctx.stdin` — so `< /dev/null` was never the fix, and closing stdin had appeared to help only because it changed nothing. Cleanup moved to `t.after`, which runs on both paths.
  <br>**The class is guarded, not just the instance.** `--test-force-exit` is in the `test` script, so a future leaked handle costs a report and an exit code instead of a timeout with no diagnostic — the failure mode that made a documented CI gate into a gate nobody ran.
- **SH146** — **a cut in `find` is a page now, not a dead end** ([ShAgentReadService](../shio-app/src/main/java/com/viglet/shio/api/agent/ShAgentReadService.java), [ShAgentFound](../shio-app/src/main/java/com/viglet/shio/api/agent/dto/ShAgentFound.java), [ShAgentAPI](../shio-app/src/main/java/com/viglet/shio/api/agent/ShAgentAPI.java), [ShFindTool](../shio-app/src/main/java/com/viglet/shio/api/agent/mcp/tools/ShFindTool.java), [agent-client.mjs](../cli/src/agent-client.mjs), [content-store.mjs](../cli/src/content-store.mjs)). A `truncated` response carries a `cursor`; `?after=<cursor>` continues the walk. A site past `shio.agent.read.max-limit` could not be projected **at all** before this — pull refused rather than write a tree whose gaps the next `--prune` would read as deletions — so the cap was the ceiling on how large a site the file projection supported.
  <br>**Keyset, never an offset**, and the sort key was already there. Content is written while the walk runs, so a post created ahead of an offset shifts every later page by one and drops a row *silently* — precisely the hole the refusal existed to prevent, reintroduced by the fix. `find` already sorts by address and an address is unique (a friendly URL is site-unique, an SH172 `id:` fallback is a UUID), so the ordering is the keyset for free and there is no second column to carry.
  <br>**The cursor is absent on the last page.** That absence is how a caller learns the walk finished, instead of having to request an empty page to find out — one fewer round trip on every complete walk, which is the common case.
  <br>**`truncated` without a cursor still means something**, and that is what keeps the safety property intact rather than trading it away: it is the pre-SH146 dead end, an instance that cannot offer one. So `readRemote` pages on the one and refuses on the other, `--allow-partial` is unchanged, and `limit` became the *page size* instead of a ceiling. `findAll` also stops when a cursor fails to advance — a server repeating one would otherwise page over the same rows forever.
  <br>**A bad cursor is a teaching 400, not an interpretation** (SH88's rule, one endpoint over). Comparing an address against `200` or a timestamp *succeeds* lexicographically and returns a plausible page, so an `after` that is not a `post:`/`id:` address is refused — a silent skip is the one failure a projection cannot detect. Blank stays "start at the beginning", since an empty query param is ordinary.
  <br>`shio_find` gains `after` (worth its schema under P3: without it an MCP-only client is back at the dead end it can see but cannot pass), the terse form puts the cursor on the **header** line for the reason SH88's feed did, and the SH130 golden was regenerated — the diff is exactly the new parameter.
- **SH149** — **an empty folder is a file** ([content-files.mjs](../cli/src/content-files.mjs), [content-store.mjs](../cli/src/content-store.mjs), [content-sync.mjs](../cli/src/content-sync.mjs), [content-pull.mjs](../cli/src/commands/content-pull.mjs), [content-push.mjs](../cli/src/commands/content-push.mjs)). `shio/folders/<site>/<name-chain>/_folder.md`, frontmatter only, declared by `push --content` as a `folder.upsert`. Before it a folder existed in the projection *only* because a post named it, so an empty section could not be authored locally and a pull dropped one that existed on the server — which meant "scaffold the structure, then fill it" had its first step outside the file tree while every other step was in it.
  <br>**A separate root, not a directory inside `shio/content`.** This is the decision the whole task turns on, and it follows from SH79: under the content root the directories are *URL* segments — `shio/content/Blog/blog/hello.md` is the post at `/blog/hello` regardless of which folder holds it — so a marker at `shio/content/Blog/blog/_folder.md` would be asserting that a URL prefix is a folder chain. The two usually agree, which is precisely what makes it dangerous: the one time they do not, the marker creates a folder nobody asked for and the real one goes unmanaged. Two roots cannot express the mistake.
  <br>**A marker declares only what nothing else does.** Writing one per folder would double a projection's file count to restate every post's own `folder:`, and each of those files would then be another thing to keep in sync. `implied` — the posts' folders plus every ancestor — is subtracted, and the skipped folders still count as *agreed* so the next pull cannot read them as deletions.
  <br>**Folders are in the base snapshot, and that is not incidental.** A marker on disk the server does not have is either a scaffold not yet pushed or a folder somebody deleted; existence alone cannot tell them apart, and each wrong guess loses real work (deleting the author's new declaration, or resurrecting a folder somebody removed). `reconcileFolders` takes the third value and decides. A snapshot written before this reads as "we have never agreed about any folder", which makes every server folder newly-added and every local marker locally-added — both safe, both self-correcting, so no version bump.
  <br>**A marker widens `--prune`'s scope, deliberately.** Declaring `/archive` means the tree owns `/archive`; the identical widening already happened the moment a *post* named it, so the marker reaches an existing rule by a different file rather than adding a rule. Documented instead of special-cased.
  <br>Two smaller refusals worth keeping: a marker whose path and `folder:` disagree is an error (SH134's lesson, which is also why it writes the two keys its path already implies), and **text in a marker is refused** rather than dropped — a folder holds posts, not prose, and silently discarding it loses something somebody wrote expecting it on the site. The folder list comes from the context pack's sitemap walked to completeness (no `GET /agent/folders` — law P10), and a walk that cannot finish marks the snapshot partial for SH146's reason: `--prune` deleting a folder takes every post beneath it.
- **SH199** — **a large tree splits, and the reason a pruning one cannot is the finding** ([content-sync.mjs](../cli/src/content-sync.mjs), [content-push.mjs](../cli/src/commands/content-push.mjs)). `splitDocuments` cuts a site's document into parts that each fit the SH138 ceiling (`--max-ops`, default 1500); the union converges exactly where the whole would have, because an upsert is independent and idempotent. Each part carries the folders and the moves — a move whose source is gone is a noop (SH150), so repeating one is free and cheaper than working out which part its post landed in.
  <br>**Both designs the task proposed turn out to be unsafe, and it is worth recording why.** *Split by declared folder subtree*: every document `documentsFor` builds declares the site root, because its folders come from `ancestorsOf`, which always yields `/` — so each part's prune is scoped to the **whole site**, and part one deletes everything part two declares. *A content pass then one pruning pass declaring every folder and no posts*: prune deletes what a document does not declare, so a pass declaring no posts deletes every post under those folders. It converges on an empty site.
