  <br>So a pruning push **stays one document**, and a tree too large for one is a teaching refusal naming `--site`, `--content-dir` or dropping `--prune` — a refusal beats a split that quietly means something else. Everything else splits, which covers the common cases: a plain push and a `--check` drift guard. `opsOf` counts the way the server counts, **publishes included**, which is the easy-to-miss part: a document of 1000 posts with `publish:` is 2000 ops, not 1000. Prune deletes are deliberately not estimated client-side — how many there are depends on what is on the server, which is one more reason a pruning document is left whole rather than split against a guess.
- **SH145** — **the bytes project too, so the tree is a complete description of a site** ([content-assets.mjs](../cli/src/content-assets.mjs), [content-store.mjs](../cli/src/content-store.mjs), [admin-client.mjs](../cli/src/admin-client.mjs), [content-pull.mjs](../cli/src/commands/content-pull.mjs), [content-push.mjs](../cli/src/commands/content-push.mjs)). Binaries live at `shio/assets/<site>/<folder-chain>/<name>` and a `File` field reads as that path instead of a UUID. Before this, three of the four things "content as files" is supposed to buy did not hold: the tree could not be moved to another instance, a diff of it was not reviewable, and it was not a complete description of the site.
  <br>**The addressing question, which the design under-specified.** Every other projection path in Block I is a friendly URL, because that is a post's identity — but a `File` post **has no friendly URL**. `ShStaticFileService.upload` never assigns one, which is precisely why SH172 had to invent the `id:` fallback. So an asset is addressed the way the server already thinks about files: its **folder chain plus its file name**, the pair `fileExists` checks and the pair the console's pre-upload check uses. That needs no change to how File posts are created and no new endpoint — the inventory is the SH62 media listing joined to the sitemap's folder chains on `folderId` (law P10: both halves already existed, nothing had put them together).
  <br>**Paths are the projection's currency; ids exist only on the wire.** This is the layering that keeps the feature from breaking the SH89 merge: an incoming `File` field is rewritten id → path *as it is read*, so the base, the server side and the file side all speak paths. Without it every File field would read as changed on every single sync, since one side would hold a UUID and the other a path. The inverse rewrite happens at one line, just before a document is compiled.
  <br>**Idempotent by path, resolved against the server rather than a memory.** A second push must not upload a second copy, and resolution is against the instance's own inventory keyed by (site, folder, file name) — not a locally remembered id — so a fresh clone with no base snapshot resolves exactly as a long-lived one does. That is SH81's `post.upsert` argument applied to bytes. **Only referenced assets upload**: a file in the tree that no `File` field names is never sent, which removes any question about what an unreferenced one means and any way for a stale one to resurrect itself.
  <br>**Two refusals and one assumption worth stating.** A declared path whose bytes are not on disk stops the push, because the alternative is publishing a post whose File field points at nothing; an upload's missing folder is created with the same `folder.upsert` the document would have used, never silently redirected to the site root. And **a path already on disk is not re-downloaded** — a File post's bytes are immutable (an upload always creates a new id-keyed post), so the same path is the same asset, and re-fetching would spend a request per image on every pull to rewrite identical bytes. An id that resolves to no known asset stays an id and is reported: the File post may be in a site this run did not read, and inventing a path would put a broken one in the tree.
  <br>Only the fields the **model** declares as `File` are touched — guessing from the shape of a value would rewrite a `Text` field that happens to hold a UUID, and nested `Relator` fields count, since an image inside a repeatable item is as much an asset as one at the top level. `--assets-dir` moves the root. Deleting an asset is deliberately not projected: bytes go when their post goes (SH38's cleanup listener), and a File post can be referenced by content this tree does not own.
- **SH148** — **the merge base is fingerprints, not a second copy of the site** ([content-sync.mjs](../cli/src/content-sync.mjs), [content-store.mjs](../cli/src/content-store.mjs), [content-pull.mjs](../cli/src/commands/content-pull.mjs), [content-push.mjs](../cli/src/commands/content-push.mjs)). `shio/.shio/content-base.json` is `version: 2` and holds a 64-bit hash per field instead of every projected value: O(fields) rather than O(content), and safe to commit — which matters because committing it is the *reasonable* choice for a team, since it makes the merge base shared, and that turned it into one extra copy of the site in every clone.
  <br>**The values were stored to be compared and then discarded.** `equal(a, b)` is `stable(a) === stable(b)`, so all three questions the merge asks — did this side change, did that side, did both — are string comparisons against the base; the merged output always takes the *remote* or *local* value; and a conflict names fields and writes nothing. Even `--show-remote` writes the server's copy, not the base's. Nothing read a base value, ever, which is what made this a pure size win rather than a trade.
  <br>**Absence needed a fingerprint of its own**, and this was the one real trap. A digest map simply has no key where a field is missing, so `undefined === undefined` — which used to be true and meant "neither the base nor this side has it" — became `undefined === <a hash>`. The effect was specific and bad: a field the server added that neither the base nor the file had came back a **conflict** instead of taking the server's value. `ABSENT` is the fingerprint of nothing, and the test for it needs *both* sides to have moved, or `reconcile` short-circuits on "only the server changed" and never reaches the per-field merge.
  <br>**A v1 snapshot is digested on read**, so an existing project keeps a working merge base with no re-pull and nothing to migrate — and since every other test in the content suite seeds a v1 fixture, the whole suite exercises that path. Two follow-on fixes fell out: `nextPosts` is uniformly digest-shaped now (`baseEntryFor`), and pull collects the folders a post declares **from the documents** rather than reading `folder` back off the base — a base entry no longer has one, and a post the file tree alone changed never gets a fresh entry, so SH149 would have written a redundant `_folder.md`. `site` and `url` stay verbatim: they are used, not compared, and a pull deletes a file by the address the base remembers.
- **SH150** — **a renamed file is a move, and the document grew one channel for intent** ([ShAgentDesiredState](../shio-app/src/main/java/com/viglet/shio/api/agent/dto/ShAgentDesiredState.java), [ShAgentDesiredStateService](../shio-app/src/main/java/com/viglet/shio/api/agent/ShAgentDesiredStateService.java), [content-sync.mjs](../cli/src/content-sync.mjs), [content-files.mjs](../cli/src/content-files.mjs), [content-push.mjs](../cli/src/commands/content-push.mjs)). A rename is two file edits — the path and `url:`, which the format already refuses to let disagree — and to a pure state document that reads as one undeclared post at the old URL plus a new post at the new. `--prune` deleted the first and created the second, so what came out had a new id and none of the original's audit trail, version history or inbound references: the workaround SH134 exists to prevent, reached from the file side.
  <br>**Why a state document needs `moves` at all.** Everything else in the document is state, and that is exactly what makes an apply re-runnable. A move is *not* state — "this post is at /b" and "this post used to be at /a" describe the same world and imply different work — so no amount of declaring could express it. `moves` is therefore the one intent channel, kept as narrow as it can be: `{from, to?, folder?}`, compiled to `post.move` **after folders and before upserts** (the destination folder must exist; the upsert must then land on the moved post rather than create a second one beside it). It stays re-runnable because a move whose `from` is gone is a **noop** — without that, pushing the same tree twice would fail on "no post at /old".
  <br>**The prune interaction is the dangerous part, and it is where the real bug would have been.** The sweep reads the database *before any op has run*, so a renamed post is still sitting at its old URL and nothing in `posts` names it — it would be swept. At apply time the move runs first and the delete would find nothing, so content would survive; but the **plan** would list `deleting post:Blog/blog/old`, and SH108's confirm digest is taken over that list. A rename would have asked the operator to confirm destroying the post it was preserving. A move's `from` now counts as declared, and its `folder` as a placement.
  <br>**Detection is three signals, in order of what they prove.** `movedFrom: <old url>` in frontmatter is an instruction like `publish:` — never written by a pull, preserved through a merge, and the only signal that survives a rename *plus* a rewrite, since after a rewrite there is nothing left to match on. Identical content (type, folder, every field) at a vanished address and a new one covers the common case — `git mv`, edit `url:`, push — with nothing asked of the author. And a `folder:` that differs from the server's is the third, which is **a defect this fixed rather than a rename**: `post.upsert` deliberately does not relocate an existing post, so editing a file's `folder:` was a push that reported success and moved nothing.
  <br>**Ambiguity is refused; probability is reported.** Two files that could each be the same rename are a one-in-two chance of moving the wrong post's history, so the push stops and names the candidates — as does a `movedFrom` pointing at a post the tree still declares. A pair that is plausible but unprovable (same type, different content) is *printed*, with the `movedFrom:` line to add, because the alternative is a delete-plus-create that destroys history in silence. A `movedFrom` equal to the file's own URL is refused at parse time: it is the likely slip (the *new* value pasted in), and left alone it compiles to a move onto itself whose server error says nothing about the actual mistake.
  <br>**Two client invariants that are easy to get wrong**, both of which turn the fix into the bug it fixes: a moved post's old address must leave `removed`, or `--prune` deletes the post the move just preserved; and it must not be re-added to the base snapshot from the server read — which was taken *before* the move — or the next run offers to prune it. Fixing the second also caught push's `writeBase` dropping SH149's folder agreement.
  <br>**Not everywhere, deliberately.** A blueprint may not declare `moves` (`CONTENT_KEYS` already refuses it): a package is an appliable *starting point*, so everything it declares is content it brings, and renaming the caller's live pages is not its business. `shio_apply` does not take it either — it is the largest tool on the surface at 437 of a 460 ceiling, and `shio_write` already carries `post.move` as one value in an op enum that exists. Same reasoning as SH151/SH152, and here the budget and the design agree.
- **SH147** — The change feed is commit-ordered: positions are reserved, not read off the clock, and a write in flight holds the feed behind it, so a slow commit cannot land past a cursor.
- **SH210** — Editing an asset's bytes now lands: push compares a path the server already has and replaces it in place, keeping the id, the folder, the name and the usage list.
- **SH211** — Renaming a folder's directory is a folder.move now: the document carries movedFrom on the folder entry, and --prune no longer deletes the section with its posts.
- **SH212** — A broken asset path is a verify finding in a projection group that reads the tree, so --checks projection is a gate with no instance and reports the whole tree at once.
- **SH213** — A push lists only the folders its File fields name — measured at 200 rows for one reference, now 10 — and an upload no longer re-reads the inventory to find one folder id.
- **SH214** — A legitimate delete-plus-create can be accepted once with push --content --accept, keyed on both addresses, and the acceptance is spent by the run that uses it.
- **SH215** — A fingerprint carries its canonical byte length, so equal hashes with unequal lengths prove a collision and the merge reports it instead of dropping the edit.
- **SH373** — Asset bytes join the SH89 merge: a server-side edit reaches the tree, a push no longer reverts one, and both sides editing is a conflict left on disk.
- **SH375** — Measured: the folderId filter ran in memory, so a folder listing read the whole library. It is a query predicate now, and the ceiling is a documented, movable latency budget.
- **SH376** — The feed says when it has met a write this node never stamped, so a two-node install stops reading as exact — proof from the position counter, with no new state.
- **SH374** — The projection group gained sidecar-missing and translation-target-missing, so two defects the tree alone proves no longer wait for a gate that needs the server.
- **SH398** — The digest is stamped at write time and rides the listing, so a settled pull went from 208 requests to 8, and a listing asks the filesystem once per row instead of twice.
- **SH399** — The size is stamped beside the digest as its validator, so bytes changed outside the CMS make the listing report no hash and recompute instead of a stale one.
- **SH400** — The write side refuses naming both paths and `verify` reports every pair as `duplicate-address`, so the `index.md` convention no longer drops a post in silence.
- **SH401** — The pull writes neither and names both, the snapshot goes partial so `--prune` cannot act, and `path-collision` catches the pair in a tree authored where the filesystem allows it.
- **SH402** — `filePathFor` refuses a URL that navigates, the pull skips and names the post instead of dying, and `skipped` now marks the snapshot partial so `--prune` cannot read a gap as a deletion.
- **SH403** — A discovery lint classifies all six path producers and lands before the fixes; it found six where three were predicted, four already guarded, and the two that were not are now skipped and named.
- **SH404** — An unscoped pull recomputes the flag from its own facts and a scoped one still inherits, so the complete projection the push tells you to take now clears what it refuses.
- **SH405** — The pull now names the truncated sitemap as the cause of a short asset inventory, says what to raise, and warns that the dangling references below may be its artefact.
- **SH406** — A first pull now scopes its asset read to the sites the posts name, so the bytes come down and the File fields become paths; the fallback is one binding shared by all three per-site reads.
- **SH407** — One collision detector now serves both roots, the pull writes neither marker and names the pair, and `verify` reads `shio/folders/` for the first time to report it with no instance.
- **SH408** — The lint now asks every root whether its outputs collide and whether a detector is wired; it named assets, post-types and site names, plus a fourth traversal gap in a module SH403 never listed.
- **SH409** — Each root now names the module whose write it guards and only that file is searched; the corrected lint named one root, and the def check moved to the loop that writes `<name>.json`.
- **SH410** — `applyBaseline` now judges staleness against what the run covered, so the server-free gate stops condemning server acceptances, and an unproven entry is `staleUnknown` rather than a build failure.
- **SH411** — `unproven` is its own list that never fails the build, `stale` still does, and `PROJECTION_RULES` is now derived from the rule literals rather than hand-kept.
- **SH412** — Both sides forgetting a note now reads as agreement and the key leaves the base, so a site's memory sync no longer freezes on a conflict that could not decay.

## Block J — Blueprints (appliable units) + Claude Code plugin (SH74)

> The block removes the *third* cost in a typical build: re-deriving a starting point that
> somebody has already derived. Design law P8 says skipping steps needs **appliable** units,
> so a blueprint is not a recipe an agent reads and reimplements — it is a package the
> instance applies, with a plan first and a proof afterwards. The section vocabulary is the
> other half of the same idea: a page made of *known* sections is a page a later session can
> change without an archaeology pass.

**Follow-ups — a package can create the site it needs, reconcile a model it does not own, and be planned without writing**

- **SH151** — **A blueprint apply can create its target site** (`createSite` on [ShBlueprintRequest](../shio-app/src/main/java/com/viglet/shio/blueprint/dto/ShBlueprintRequest.java), [ShSiteWriteService#createBlank](../shio-app/src/main/java/com/viglet/shio/api/site/ShSiteWriteService.java), `shio apply --create-site`). *"One call builds a marketing site"* was one call only if a site already existed to apply it into, and the only creation path cloned the SH71 bootstrap template — so "create a site for this package" meant applying a package on top of a Welcome page nobody asked for and then pruning it. Hence a **blank** site path, which is worth having on its own: the clone exists because an empty site used to be useless, and a blueprint is exactly the thing that makes it useful.
  <br>**The default stays a refusal.** Creating a site is the most visible side effect in the system, so it is requested, never inferred from "the site you named does not exist" (P7). What changed is that the refusal now *names both routes* — the flag, and a `site.upsert` op — instead of pointing at `POST /api/v2/site`.
  <br>**A plan creates it inside the transaction it rolls back**, the same technique the post-type half already uses and for the same reason: without the site, the content planner cannot resolve a single address, so a plan for a not-yet-existing site could not be a plan at all. Nothing survives the return, and the test asserts that.
- **SH152** — **Additive post-type reconciliation** (`mergePostTypes`, [ShPostTypeAdminService#mergeMissingFields](../shio-app/src/main/java/com/viglet/shio/api/post/type/ShPostTypeAdminService.java), [ShPostTypeMergeTest](../shio-app/src/test/java/com/viglet/shio/api/post/type/ShPostTypeMergeTest.java)). A package's post-type that already exists was left alone and its missing fields *reported* — honest, and one step short of useful. **SH168 made it worse than that**: those content writes are now refused rather than silently mangled, so the report named a wall instead of a wart. The opt-in merge adds the fields the package declares and the type lacks, and nothing else: never changes a widget or its settings, never removes a field, never reorders, never touches a system type. Every one of those exclusions is something somebody else may own.
  <br>**Two decisions, both visible in the tests.** An added field's **ordinal is appended** after the highest existing one — honouring the package's own ordinals would push a human's field down their form. And the report says **`merge`** with the fields it `added`, because a merge that read as a provision would hide that the type is now a hybrid of two models, which is exactly what somebody debugging the form six months later needs to know.
- **SH170** — **`site.upsert`: the batch surface can make a site** ([ShAgentBatchService](../shio-app/src/main/java/com/viglet/shio/api/agent/ShAgentBatchService.java)). Seven ops could build everything inside a site and none could make one, so an agent asked for the thing the product is *for* found that step one was not here — and landed on the console entity API: id-keyed, entity-shaped and CSRF-gated, which answers a stateless caller with a bodiless 403. Nothing to read, nothing to fix. The eighth op is addressed (`site:<name>`), idempotent, and creates a **blank** site.
  <br>**It never updates**, deliberately: the name is the address, and a site's URL, description and layout are console concerns with a human looking at them. An "upsert" that quietly repointed a live site's URL because a document mentioned it would be the surprise P7 forbids — so it creates or reports `noop`, and says which. **It refuses a scoped credential**: a token with an SH2 site allow-list may not invent a site outside it, which would make the allow-list "sites this token may read, plus any it makes up".
  <br>**Not on the MCP tool schema, and that is the interesting part.** `createSite` on `shio_apply` measured 18 tokens over the per-tool ceiling and pushed `tools/list` over its total — a bill every session pays on every turn, including the ones that never create a site (P3). It is not needed there: `shio_write` takes `site.upsert` for free, because it is one more value in an `op` enum that already existed, and the missing-site error names it. The manifest advertises `siteUpsert` so nobody has to discover it by reading the Java.
- **SH153** — **A blueprint plan needs no write transaction** (`ShAgentBatchService.Declared`, [ShAgentBatchService](../shio-app/src/main/java/com/viglet/shio/api/agent/ShAgentBatchService.java), [ShBlueprintWriteService](../shio-app/src/main/java/com/viglet/shio/blueprint/ShBlueprintWriteService.java), [ShPostTypeAdminService#mergeableFieldNames](../shio-app/src/main/java/com/viglet/shio/api/post/type/ShPostTypeAdminService.java)). The plan used to provision the package's post-types — and, after SH151, its site — inside its own transaction and mark it rollback-only. It was accurate, and the justification held: provisioning a post-type emits no audit rows, no webhooks, no lifecycle events and no quota movement, so nothing outside the transaction observed it. What it cost is a property nobody asked to give up — **a plan could not run read-only**: not on a read-only credential, not on a replica, not inside a `readOnly` transaction. On a surface whose entire safety story is *look before you write*, that is the wrong constraint to leave standing.
  <br>**The fix is the pending set, one resource wider.** The dry run already keeps the folders earlier ops *would* have created, precisely so "create /blog, then put a post in /blog" does not report a spurious 404. `Declared` is the same idea for the site and the post-types: the caller states what its own run would create, and the plan resolves against it. A declared site is a stand-in with a name and **no id**, which is what every lookup keys on — no root folder, no folders, no posts — so each op below it plans as a create, which is exactly true of a site that does not exist yet.
  <br>**Two rules keep a declaration from becoming a lie.** It is **additive, never a substitute**: a post-type that really exists is still resolved live and the declared names are *unioned* with its own. So with `mergePostTypes` off, nothing is declared for an existing type and SH168's `undeclared field(s) … a real run will refuse this write` survives — a plan may never be greener than the run it predicts, and there is a test whose whole job is that sentence. And it is **honoured on a dry run only** (`Session` discards it otherwise), so a declaration can never stand in for a write that did not happen; the id on a declared post-type is `null`, which makes the wrong path a crash rather than a silent create against a type that does not exist.
  <br>**What proves it.** `ShBlueprintWriteService.plan` is `@Transactional(readOnly = true)` and the test runs a whole plan inside a read-only `TransactionTemplate` — the old implementation could not have. Asserting the post-type is *absent* afterwards only ever proved nothing survived; this proves nothing was attempted. `mergeMissingFields` and the new read-only `mergeableFieldNames` now share one notion of what is missing, so a plan cannot promise a field the apply skips.
- **SH155** — **A site records which package built it** ([ShBlueprintRecord](../shio-app/src/main/java/com/viglet/shio/blueprint/ShBlueprintRecord.java), `recordedAs` on [ShBlueprintApplied](../shio-app/src/main/java/com/viglet/shio/blueprint/dto/ShBlueprintApplied.java), [ShBlueprintRecordTest](../shio-app/src/test/java/com/viglet/shio/blueprint/ShBlueprintRecordTest.java)). `changed: 0` on a re-apply proved a site matched the document a package compiles to; nothing recorded that the document *came from* `marketing-site 1.0.0`. So a newer package version was undetectable, "which blueprint is this site" was unanswerable, and the version in the apply response survived only in whatever transcript happened to capture it.
  <br>**A memory note, not a table** — the design's own call, and it earns it twice. This is exactly a decision about the site that a later session should not have to re-derive, which is what SH114's store is *for*; and memory rides the context pack's `conventions`, so the next session learns what the site is made of in the call it already makes (P2). A table would have needed an endpoint, a client, and a reason to read it.
  <br>**One note per package, keyed `blueprint.<name>`.** A site can receive a `landing` and then a `blog`, so a single `blueprint` key would make the second apply erase the first. Keyed by name, a re-apply rewrites its own row (upsert by `(scope, key)`, so the record cannot grow) and a second package adds one — "what is this site made of" is the set of `blueprint.*` notes scoped to it. A package name that is not a valid slug records **nothing** rather than a sanitised guess: a third-party package (SH96) with such a name has a problem the record must not hide behind a key nobody can search for.
  <br>**Three smaller decisions.** Parameters are **sorted** and `site` is dropped — the same apply has to write the same bytes, or the note rewrites itself and its date stops meaning "when this was last confirmed" (P5), and the reserved parameter always equals the note's own scope. A list too long for the 400-character budget says **how many it dropped**, because an unreported cut reads as "these were all the parameters" (SH138's rule). And a **failed note leaves the apply standing**: it is written after the writer's transaction, next to `verify`, so destroying a site's worth of committed content over a 200-character annotation is not a trade the code can make — the response simply does not claim a record it does not have.
- **SH156** — **The section packages carry their front-end half** ([create-shio-app/src/emit.mjs](../create-shio-app/src/emit.mjs), [shio-sections/front-end/](../shio-sections/front-end/), [emit.test.mjs](../create-shio-app/test/emit.test.mjs), [publish-js-sdk.yml](../.github/workflows/publish-js-sdk.yml)). `landing` and `marketing-site` delivered content the site could not render until somebody installed `@viglet/shio-sections` and wrote the page that resolves a `Page`'s section URLs — a dozen lines an agent had to produce from a description, which is the prose recipe P8 objects to. `shio init --blueprint landing` said it out loud: *"carries no front-end files, so there is nothing to scaffold"*.
  <br>**The prerequisite nobody had noticed.** `@viglet/shio-sections` and `@viglet/shio-model` were **not published** — the release workflow shipped four packages and not those two. Both are packaged to be published (`dist`, `files`, `prepublishOnly`), so this was an omission rather than a decision, and it made the whole feature impossible: a package carrying a page that imports the vocabulary would produce a project whose `npm install` fails. A vocabulary meant to be *one shared language for the agent, the console and the front end* (SH95) that nobody can install is not shared. Both now publish, first and in dependency order, because `shio-sections` resolves `shio-model` through `workspace:*`.
  <br>**How packages share a tree, answered: they each carry a copy and nobody writes one.** `emit` grew from one target to a list, and composes each package's tree as *the starter plus an overlay* — replace-by-path, so the section-aware catch-all **is** `app/[...slug]/page.tsx` rather than a second route the project must be told about, plus one `lib/sections.ts` resolver and a merged `package.json` dependency whose range is read from the workspace (a hardcoded one would point generated projects at a version nobody published). A hand-maintained second starter drifts within a release; a generated one cannot, and a test asserts the overlay changes **exactly three files** — if that list grows, the overlay has become a fork.
  <br>**One route serves both kinds of page**, and it decides by what the content declares rather than by which blueprint built the site: a page whose `sections` field names other posts is composed with `<Sections>`, anything else falls back to the single HTML field. A section URL that resolves to nothing is **dropped, not placeheld** — it is a real defect with an owner (`shio verify`'s `dangling-reference`), and rendering the CMS's diagnostics on a visitor's page reports it a second time in the one place nobody can act on it.
  <br>**Scoped honestly.** `blog`, `docs` and `product-catalog` are **not** included and the code says why: they do not compose sections, so the overlay would ship them a dependency they never import. What they actually lack is an *index* page over their own content, which is per-package — filed as **SH216**. Two smaller things fell out: the section packages had to declare `projectName` (the registry refuses a `{{placeholder}}` with no parameter behind it — the author-error guard working exactly as designed), and `emit`'s `import.meta.url === \`file://${process.argv[1]}\`` guard **never fired on Windows**, so running the generator did nothing at all, silently. It uses `pathToFileURL` now.
- **SH96 (local half)** — **A package may come from a directory an operator named** (`shio.blueprint.path`, [ShBlueprintProperties](../shio-app/src/main/java/com/viglet/shio/blueprint/ShBlueprintProperties.java), [ShBlueprintRegistry](../shio-app/src/main/java/com/viglet/shio/blueprint/ShBlueprintRegistry.java), [ShBlueprintLocalPathTest](../shio-app/src/test/java/com/viglet/shio/blueprint/ShBlueprintLocalPathTest.java)). The registry loaded from the classpath alone, deliberately: a blueprint is code the instance runs against its own content — it provisions a model, writes pages, and with the SH151/SH152 opt-ins creates a site and edits an existing post-type — so *where may a package come from* is a trust question, and shipping a scanned directory or a URL before answering it would have been shipping the distribution channel without the trust model.
  <br>**The model is the smallest one that is actually a model: an operator names a directory.** Whoever can set that property can already put a jar on the classpath, so it grants no authority that did not exist — it makes the existing authority usable without repackaging. The person who set it is the person vouching for what is in it, which is a sentence with a subject; *"packages resolve from npm"* is not, and that is the difference between this half and the one still open.
  <br>**Three refusals, each guarding a way this could quietly go wrong.** A **name collision fails at load** naming both origins, because neither winner is defensible: shadowing would change what every existing `blog` apply does with nothing saying so, and ignoring would make the operator's package do nothing. A **configured path that is not a readable directory fails** rather than yielding an empty result — a typo that degraded silently to "the first-party set" is how a site gets built from the wrong packages and nobody finds out until they read the content. And **the same validation runs**, so "it loaded" means the same thing whichever source it came from; a directory must not be a way to smuggle a package past the checks the format exists for.
  <br>**Every package remembers its origin**, reported on the listing for local ones only — an agent about to write to somebody's site should be able to tell that the package it picked did not ship with the CMS (P7), while stamping `"classpath"` on six first-party rows would spend tokens on every listing to say "normal" (P3). A stray subdirectory with no manifest is skipped rather than refused: an operator's package folder is a working directory, and a `.git` is not a malformed package.
  <br>**What is still open is the community half** — a naming convention, a curated index, and some notion of provenance stronger than "an operator put it there". That is **SH217**; this ships the local trust model it needs to sit on.

- **SH92** — **Blueprint package format** ([com.viglet.shio.blueprint](../shio-app/src/main/java/com/viglet/shio/blueprint)). A package is a directory with a [ShBlueprintManifest](../shio-app/src/main/java/com/viglet/shio/blueprint/dto/ShBlueprintManifest.java) (`blueprint.json`), post-type files, content documents, optional front-end files and a `verify` promise. **Nothing in it is a new serialization:** `postTypes` are SH16 `ShPostTypeDef`s (the JSON `shio pull` writes, so a package's model can be authored with `@viglet/shio-model` and diffed with `shio push --check`) and `content` files are SH82 desired-state documents, which is what keeps the format from becoming a third contract (P10). The design calls worth naming: (1) **a package may not name its own site** — the site is the caller's, so the common case (apply *into* an existing instance) works and a `site` key in a content document is refused at load rather than ignored, because an ignored key looks like it worked; (2) **a package may not `prune`** — prune's blast radius depends on what the document's author forgot to mention (P7) and that author is a package the user did not write; (3) **parameters are a JSON Schema, and substitution is `{{name}}` and nothing else** — no conditionals, no expressions, because every one of those turns a package from data into a program whose output cannot be predicted by reading it (P5); (4) **`site` is a reserved parameter**, always available, never declarable. [ShBlueprintParams](../shio-app/src/main/java/com/viglet/shio/blueprint/ShBlueprintParams.java) makes every parameter mistake a teaching 400 with `allowed`/`didYouMean` — an unknown parameter is *refused*, not ignored, since a silently-dropped `brandName` yields a site full of defaults with nothing to suspect. **The load-time validation is the part that matters** ([ShBlueprintRegistry](../shio-app/src/main/java/com/viglet/shio/blueprint/ShBlueprintRegistry.java)): a referenced file that is not in the package, a path that escapes it, an unknown manifest key, a `{{placeholder}}` with no declared parameter, and a `verify.posts` entry the package's own content never declares are all the *author's* mistakes, and all of them would otherwise surface as a stranger's half-applied site. A malformed package is a **409, not a 400** — nothing the caller sent caused it, and a 400 would send an agent into a retry loop over its own arguments. [ShBlueprintCodec](../shio-app/src/main/java/com/viglet/shio/blueprint/ShBlueprintCodec.java) carries the same `FAIL_ON_NULL_FOR_PRIMITIVES=false` decision `ShExchangePackageCodec` made for SH68 and for the same reason: the canonical authoring form omits delivered-only fields (`managed`), and Jackson 3 rejects an absent primitive by default. 8 tests ([ShBlueprintRegistryTest](../shio-app/src/test/java/com/viglet/shio/blueprint/ShBlueprintRegistryTest.java), no Spring context — it runs in milliseconds so it can run on every change to a package) + 8 ([ShBlueprintParamsTest](../shio-app/src/test/java/com/viglet/shio/blueprint/ShBlueprintParamsTest.java)). → was §XI.1
- **SH93** — **Applying one** (`GET /api/v2/agent/blueprints`, `GET /agent/blueprints/{name}`, `POST /agent/blueprints/{name}/apply`, `shio blueprints`, `shio apply --blueprint`, and `blueprint`/`params` on `shio_apply`). [ShBlueprintService](../shio-app/src/main/java/com/viglet/shio/blueprint/ShBlueprintService.java) resolves the parameters, substitutes them, compiles the result into a post-type list plus **one** merged desired-state document (one document, so a package cannot half-apply and the compiler's folders-then-posts-then-publishes ordering holds), and hands both to [ShBlueprintWriteService](../shio-app/src/main/java/com/viglet/shio/blueprint/ShBlueprintWriteService.java). Four decisions: (1) **the model is provisioned, never upserted** — `provisionFromDef` leaves an existing post-type exactly as it is, including a field a human added, because a blueprint seeds a model and does not own one; upserting would also flip SH66's `managed` flag and lock the type in the console from a package the user never wrote; (2) **the plan provisions inside its transaction and rolls back** — the content planner resolves every post's type against the live model, so without this a plan for a package bringing its own types would fail on its first post with "no post-type named Article" and be useless for exactly the case blueprints exist for. This is the technique `ShAgentBatchService` *refuses* for content, and the difference is real rather than convenient: content writes emit audit rows, webhooks, lifecycle events and quota movements that a rollback cannot take back, while provisioning a post-type emits none of those. The content half of the plan is still a true dry run and writes nothing at all — the test asserts the post-type is **absent** afterwards, which is the only way to see it; (3) **a name collision is reported, not resolved** — a site created through the console already carries the SH71 bootstrap `Page` (`title` + `content`) while the section vocabulary's `Page` has `sections`, so the older type wins and the response names the fields it lacks, because the alternative is content written into a field the console cannot render (**SH152** reconciles); (4) **the front-end files are returned, never written** — they belong in the caller's project and the server cannot see a working tree, so `shio apply --blueprint` writes them (never over an existing file without `--force`) and an MCP-only caller is told what it has *not* got (P9). 6 end-to-end tests ([ShBlueprintApplyTest](../shio-app/src/test/java/com/viglet/shio/blueprint/ShBlueprintApplyTest.java)) + 11 CLI ([blueprints.test.mjs](../cli/test/blueprints.test.mjs)). → was §XI.2
- **SH94** — **First-party set**: `blog` (an Article type, `/blog`, three published samples), `docs` (a DocPage type and a `/docs` tree with guides and reference), `product-catalog` (a Product type with SKU, price and a Relator spec list, plus an accessories subsection), `marketing-site` (home, pricing and about, each composed of sections) and `landing` (one campaign page of four sections) — [shio-app/src/main/resources/blueprints](../shio-app/src/main/resources/blueprints). Every package declares a `verify` promise, and the promise is checked **twice**: at load against the package's own content (so a promise nobody could keep never ships) and after an apply against the instance, alongside the SH99 lint over the target site. That second check is reported rather than rolled back — the content apply is already atomic and re-applying converges, so the useful answer to "it promised /pricing and it is not there" is a report the caller can act on plus the findings that usually explain why. A required parameter is used where a package genuinely cannot invent a value (`brand`, `productName`) and a default where it can (`blogTitle`, `currency`); `shio apply --blueprint` exits **non-zero** when the verification fails, so an unattended apply cannot report success it did not earn. → was §XI.3
- **SH95** — **Section library** ([`@viglet/shio-sections`](../shio-sections)) — the highest-leverage item in the block, and the one that makes *changing* a site cheap rather than archaeological. Eight post-types (`Page` plus `SectionHero`, `SectionFeatureGrid`, `SectionCta`, `SectionLogoWall`, `SectionTestimonial`, `SectionFaq`, `SectionRichText`) authored with `@viglet/shio-model` in [post-types.ts](../shio-sections/src/post-types.ts), and the matching React components in [components.tsx](../shio-sections/src/components.tsx) with a `SECTION_COMPONENTS` registry and a `<Sections>` dispatcher. **The composition rule:** a `Page` names its sections by **friendly URL, in order**, in a Multi Select — not by id (SH79 exists so no UUID has to survive between calls), and not as a Relator (whose children are one fixed shape, while a page's sections are deliberately heterogeneous). **The components are unstyled and semantic on purpose:** they ship the *structure* — heading level, landmark, alt text — and leave design to the site's CSS via stable `shio-*` class names, because a package that shipped opinions about type scale would be replaced on day one, and because SH101's digest reads structure, so a shared vocabulary is only verifiable if structure is the shared part. `<Sections>` takes **resolved** sections rather than fetching them, so the vocabulary works from a server component, a loader or a static build. The definitions ship into the two blueprints that use them as canonical JSON (a running instance reads packages off the classpath and cannot run a JS build), generated by [scripts/emit.mjs](../shio-sections/scripts/emit.mjs) and guarded by [emit.test.mjs](../shio-sections/test/emit.test.mjs) — two copies of anything eventually disagree, so the second is generated and the build fails the moment they diverge. 12 tests, including a source-level guard that every section post-type has a component and that every `<img>` the vocabulary renders carries `alt`. → was §XI.4
- **SH97** — **Claude Code plugin** ([claude-plugin/](../claude-plugin), published through the repo-root [marketplace](../.claude-plugin/marketplace.json)): `claude plugin marketplace add openviglet/shio && claude plugin install shio`. An MCP server entry that runs the CLI's stdio bridge through `npx` (nothing to install first), three skills — `shio-site` (addressing, `shio_apply`, draft-then-publish, moves), `shio-content-model` (post-types as code, the widget list, the traps) and `shio-verify` (how to read the lint's severities, digests, the bounded incident window) — three commands (`/shio-start`, `/shio-blueprint`, `/shio-check`), and an `AGENTS.fragment.md` for projects whose sessions will not have the plugin. This is the **distribution channel for the whole concept**: it is how a developer adopts agent-native Shio in one command, and what the skills encode are the rules that are expensive to learn by making the mistake (path addressing, plan before write, DRAFT by default, `post.move` for a rename, verify before reporting done). The fragment says out loud that it is hand-written and will rot, and points at SH115. 6 tests ([plugin.test.mjs](../claude-plugin/test/plugin.test.mjs)) validate the manifests, that the marketplace's `source` exists, that every skill's description states its trigger (the description is the *only* thing that decides whether a skill loads), that no command that writes omits `dryRun` or the DRAFT rule, and that no credential is defaulted in `.mcp.json`. → was §XI.6
- **Block J wiring** — manifest: `blueprints` flips to `true` (reported `false` through Blocks H, K and I so that flipping it would mean a real registry rather than an intention), two endpoints join the curated index, and the blueprint hint folds into the existing write step so `startHere` stays five lines. MCP: `shio_apply` gains `blueprint` + `params` rather than an eleventh tool — "converge to this document" and "converge to this package" are one decision with two inputs, and a `shio_blueprint` of its own would have cost more schema than the two arguments did while making "which tool" a question the model has to answer; the new `shio://blueprints` resource is the catalogue, terse and without per-package schemas so choosing between five packages does not cost five schemas. The SH132 budgets rise for it (`max-per-tool` 400 → 460, `total` 2110 → 2160, both justified in [token-budgets.properties](../shio-app/src/test/resources/token-budgets.properties)) and the SH130 golden was regenerated — the diff is exactly the two new parameters and the new resource. The `new-site` and `add-section` MCP prompts now check the catalogue *before* modelling by hand, because a procedure that omits that step teaches the agent to pay Block J's cost anyway. CLI: `shio blueprints [name]` and `shio apply --blueprint` with `--param`/`--params`/`--site`/`--force`; `parseArgs` gained a `repeatable` option so a repeated `--param` is collected rather than reduced to the last one, which would apply a package with defaults the caller believed they had overridden. Parameter values are coerced against the package's **declared** types (a terminal has only strings) rather than by guessing from their shape, which would send a version number or a SKU as a number.
- **SH447** — init --blueprint gains the --param/--params flags it never had (one parser with apply, in blueprint-params.mjs) and checks the required-and-absent ones before writeProjectFiles rather than after the fifteen files - restating the server's rule exactly, and only when a --site is given, so the refusal moves earlier without widening. Validated rather than reported, because printing what landed still leaves the directory that blocks the retry. Running it against a live instance found the same defect with a second trigger: an absent --site also refused after the write, and the createSite remedy the server names was one init could not express, so --create-site exists here too and an absent site is a teaching refusal before the write.
- **SH595** — `/shio-start` reads `shio://manifest` first and reports the `features` that are **false** and the `limits` — what an assumption gets wrong — then `shio_remember`, before it touches the model, the packages or the lint state. The assertion is about *order*, because the defect was: nothing was missing, so a test looking only for the string would pass on a file that reads the manifest last, and `plugin.test.mjs` compares its position against every other call the command makes. The replication procedure moved with it — 223 lines that existed in one clone became the `shio-replicate` skill every installation inherits, keeping only what is true of any instance.
- **SH216** — The open question was where a per-package overlay lives, and the answer is create-shio-app/overlays/<name>/: the section overlay sits in shio-sections because the vocabulary owns how it renders, and these have no vocabulary - so the owner is whoever owns the starter. Not beside the blueprint, which was the tempting answer, because blueprints/<name>/files/ is the tree emit writes and a source overlay there would put input and output in one directory. Each package carries one page the starter cannot: a post list, a documentation tree, a catalogue grid - three shapes, which is why it is three overlays. None declares needs, which is the whole distinction from the section overlay.
- **SH217** — Built the property the community half needs before it needs an index: a local package that will not load is refused ON ITS OWN and named, so a package the operator did not write cannot take the catalogue down with it. Measured rather than imagined - during SH216 one first-party manifest missing one parameter made GET /agent/blueprints answer 4xx for all six packages and failed 41 tests. A first-party failure still fails the registry, which is the same rule read from both sides: a failure is isolated exactly when its author is somebody the operator did not choose to trust. A collision still throws, because that is a conflict about what a name means rather than one package's problem. Distribution - the naming convention, the curated index, the provenance signal - is SH643.
- **SH218** — Half of this was already built - the release re-runs emit and commits the trees - so what shipped is the half the section's last sentence names: a job that regenerates content should fail loudly if the regeneration changes something it did not expect. It does not. The drift test answers 'the tree matches its source' on a PUSH, which is after the release committed, so the one moment nobody reads emit's output is the one where a job writes into shio-app/src/main/resources/ and commits it in the same breath. The rule is about files rather than lines: a release changes versions, and a generated file appearing or disappearing is an overlay somebody edited without running emit, landing in the one commit nobody reviews.
- **SH219** — An explicit admin reload rather than a watcher, which is the same argument SH96 makes about the directory: the trust model is that somebody decided. A watcher would re-run validation at a moment nobody chose, so a half-saved manifest would change what the catalogue says between two applies - an author's editing state becoming every caller's problem. SH217 shrank that failure without removing it, and the reload answers with the loaded count and the refusals, which closes the author's loop in one call: drop the package in, reload, read why it was refused. It rebuilds rather than merges, so a package the operator deleted stops being appliable.
- **SH220** — A re-apply now defaults to SH155's record, and says which values it defaulted - the load-bearing half, because a parameter silently supplied is one nobody reviews. An explicit --param always wins: the record is a default, not a policy, or the site becomes unchangeable through the command that changes it. The hazard the section did not name is that the note is prose bounded at 400 characters and admits a cut with (+n more); a parser that dropped that admission would supply some parameters and omit others, which is the same defect arriving from the other side. The format now lives in two languages, so ShBlueprintRecordTest pins the sentence and names the CLI file to change with it.
- **SH221** — The section proposed a readOnly transaction and that was the right instinct with the wrong instrument, for two reasons found by trying to scope it. The entry points are shared - all three run overloads serve plan and apply, dryRun is a body field, and dispatching to a second annotated method from inside the service is a self-invocation that never crosses the proxy. And readOnly does not mean the same thing on the three engines this product supports: PostgreSQL refuses the write, H2 and MariaDB accept a connection merely advertised as read-only, so the guarantee would hold where CI runs Postgres and nowhere else. Counting the mutations Hibernate performed is engine-independent and states the property directly, with a third case proving the counter sees a real write.
- **SH395** — The blocker was not authoring: a blueprint parameter and a Handlebars expression are both curly-braced, so the format refused any layout at load and at substitution. Lifted inside the render fields only. Two more gaps behind it - render.provision was reachable only by naming SH95 vocabulary, so a document that WRITES a template could not ask for the type that template is of, and a plan then refused on a post-type the same plan would have created, which is SH153 one type-family along. blog now ships a Theme, a PageLayout and a binding, and the assertion renders the applied site rather than counting its content.
- **SH518** — The generator was on the replication path: convert writes a Theme and a PageLayout, so a blueprint-built site answered 400 on /preview and getting one to render meant harvesting those posts from a throwaway conversion. Declared in the packages rather than generated in Java, because SH395 made a package able to carry its design and a blueprint stays a declaration of content - and because a converter's layout is for replication fidelity while a package's is a designed starting point, so sharing them would couple the two. marketing-site and landing now ship a section-rendering layout, and the assertion renders the applied page and finds data-shio-prop on it.
- **SH604** — The README listed ten tools and four resources against eleven and seven, so shio_remember and shio://diagnostics had both shipped and the plugin never learned either - the two that cost most, in the artefact a new installation reads first. The rule is not to regenerate the list: naming a tool to teach a rule is teaching and enumerating them is a copy, so the guard refuses three or more on one line and every skill and command passes it unchanged. The enumeration is gone in favour of routing to shio://manifest, which is right by construction where a README is right until the next release.
- **SH605** — The box is taken from npm pack rather than from a list, so it cannot drift from the files field or from a directory somebody added, and five assertions ask what a stranger holding only it can do: no reader-facing file names a repo-only path, every relative link resolves inside the box, the box names a first move on each of the three surfaces, the walk is not empty, and nothing tells a reader to run a command only a checkout has. It came back GREEN, which the section did not expect - the repo-local skills turn out to be contributor-facing while the plugin's four are usage-facing, so the split was already right. Proved non-vacuous by planting a leak: three of the five fire.
- **SH643** — The code half: the bounds an applied package is held to, stated once and asserted, and the shio-blueprint- prefix reserved so it can mean something. Every bound already existed and none was anywhere they were true together - they lived in six comments across four classes, which is a security model somebody has to reconstruct by reading the implementation. Writing it found a published claim my own SH395 had made false: the end-user page said an unknown parameter is never quietly dropped, which stopped being true inside template fields. The index and the provenance signal are deferred as SH646, because there is no third-party package and an index with nothing to index is infrastructure ahead of its problem.
- **SH646** — GET /api/v2/marketplace answers what this instance could install, off by default and behind a URL the operator names - so the catalogue is a distribution channel for what SH96 already accepts rather than a second way in. The built-in six are derived from the registry rather than restated, an unreachable or malformed catalogue becomes a reported state beside them instead of an empty listing, and the README proxy fetches only a URL the catalogue itself declares, which is an exact allow-list where a scheme check would be a guess.
- **SH675** — POST /api/v2/marketplace/{id}/install downloads, expands into shio.blueprint.path and reloads, with dryRun and an uninstall beside it; the reload happens inside the install, so a package the registry refuses is rolled back rather than left behind reporting success. The refusals only a download can need are teaching errors - a zip entry escaping its directory, a manifest name disagreeing with the catalogue id, an archive with no manifest, a name already taken - and the two writes are classified CONSOLE_ADMIN, because planting a package the registry will load on every later apply is the operator decision the catalogue already made them the subject of.
- **SH676** — shio-site/scripts/marketplace.mjs derives the catalogue and one deterministic zip per package from the blueprints the jar already carries, and the site build runs it so the Pages workflow publishes it - the archives are gitignored rather than committed. The six go out as shio-blueprint-<name> because the catalogue drops a remote entry colliding with a built-in one, so under their own names every entry would be discarded everywhere; the manifest inside each zip is rewritten to match, since the installer refuses a package that disagrees with the catalogue about its own name. Proved by installing one into a live instance from the generated tree served on loopback.
- **SH677** — shio marketplace list|show|install|uninstall over the Basic auth the CLI already carries, so the capability is not console-only: the writes left sessionRequired() the way render did, because holding a session identifies a browser rather than an operator. A 404 on this surface throws instead of becoming an empty answer, since the two 404s here are the most instructive refusals the marketplace has, and show fetches the README through the instance, which proxies only a URL its own catalogue declares. Driving it live found the catalogue reporting an installed third-party package as built-in, fixed to read the origin.
- **SH678** — shio_marketplace is the twelfth tool: it lists what this instance could install and shows one in detail, and it deliberately cannot install, because MCP tools call services in process and an API token reaching /mcp is barred from /api/v2/marketplace - so an install verb would hand that token what the URL layer denies it. The tool measures 96 tokens and took tools/list to 2493, so the ceiling rose to 2500; the trim came first and found nothing in shio_apply or shio_write, but did find a sentence in the new tool restating another tool schema, which paid 15 of the 93.
- **SH679** — The console has a marketplace page: a filterable grid, a detail dialog carrying the package parameters and its README, a dry run, install and uninstall, under Administration because it installs software rather than authoring anything. The opt-ins a package declares are an amber consent panel rather than a badge, since P7 is about the surprise and not the label, and a refusal shows the server teaching sentence rather than a status. Verified in a real browser: the dry run reported nothing was written, and an install put the package on disk.
- **SH682** — The marketplace install and uninstall are hasRole("ADMIN") on both chains, with the assertion SH677 could not write: a non-admin is refused and the seeded admin is not.
- **SH881** — Both packages provision SectionMarkup now, and a check holds directory and manifest together both ways; landing already provisioned three unused types, which settled the direction.
- **SH884** — Both package layouts annotate the page's own title where they draw it and declare description in a hidden element, so a curator can edit the page as well as its sections.

## Block M — Token economy, measured (SH74)

> The brief asks that this get cheaper over time, so the block's job was to stop asserting
> it. Every number below is produced by the build: what a canonical job costs, what each
> canonical response costs, and how much of both an agent avoids paying twice. The one
> place the measurement disagrees with the concept spec is recorded as a task rather than
> rounded off.
>
> **The block closed with SH157–SH161 and SH174**, all six of them opened by the measurement
> itself. The numbers now read **tokens 2.8×–10.5×, tool calls 2.3×–3.8×** — and SH157 is the
> first change in three blocks to move a ratio by improving the *agent* path rather than by
> the baseline getting leaner.

- **SH112** — **Task benchmark harness** ([ShAgentTaskBenchmarkTest](../shio-app/src/test/java/com/viglet/shio/api/agent/benchmark/ShAgentTaskBenchmarkTest.java), [ShAgentBenchmark](../shio-app/src/test/java/com/viglet/shio/api/agent/benchmark/ShAgentBenchmark.java)). Four canonical jobs — build a marketing site, add a post-type and ten posts, fix a broken link, translate a site — each run **twice**: once over the agent surface and once over the same instance's id-keyed console/CDA endpoints, the way a client without addressing, batching or a context pack would have to. **The baseline is the point.** A single-path benchmark only says whether today is worse than yesterday; the ratio is what makes the claim falsifiable. Calls, tokens (request *and* response — a batch of ten posts spends most of its cost upward, and counting only responses would make a chatty writer look cheap) and wall clock are recorded; calls, tokens and both ratios are asserted against ceilings in [token-budgets.properties](../shio-app/src/test/resources/token-budgets.properties); **wall clock is recorded and never asserted**, because CI timing is noise at this scale and a benchmark that fails on noise gets deleted. The run is written to `target/agent-benchmark.json` so a release can archive it.
  <br>**What it measured (2026.3):** tokens **3.8×–23.3×** cheaper on the agent path, so the ≈10× target is met on three tasks of four — the fourth is the blueprint apply, which also provisions eight post-types the hand-built baseline assumes into existence, and the comparison is left understating the agent path rather than adjusted to flatter it. Tool calls: **1.8×–3.3×** against a ≈6× target, **not met anywhere**. The floors in the properties file are set at what the surface actually achieves, not at what the spec asked for, because a ceiling nothing can pass is a ceiling somebody disables; the gap itself is **SH157**.
  <br>**What driving the write surface over real HTTP found:** Jackson 3 enables `FAIL_ON_NULL_FOR_PRIMITIVES` by default, and for a *record* an absent property reaches the canonical constructor as a null — so the most natural call the protocol has, `POST /api/v2/agent/batch {"ops":[…]}` without `dryRun`, answered **400 "Request body could not be read"** without naming a field. Same for a blueprint apply without `dryRun` and a post-type definition without `system`. It broke P2 and P6 at once and was invisible to every test that builds the request record in Java, which is how it survived Blocks H, I, J and K. Fixed in [application.properties](../shio-app/src/main/resources/application.properties) and mirrored into the test properties — which *shadow* the main file rather than merging with it, the drift that let it hide (**SH158** guards the class).
- **SH113** — **Response budget enforcement** ([ShAgentResponseBudgetTest](../shio-app/src/test/java/com/viglet/shio/api/agent/benchmark/ShAgentResponseBudgetTest.java)). Eleven canonical responses measured through the instance's own `X-Shio-Est-Tokens` (SH124) — not re-tokenized locally, or the number an operator logs and the number CI guards would be two different numbers with only one of them checked — against ceilings in the same `token-budgets.properties` SH132 already uses. It is the cheap always-on guard between benchmark runs, and what it defends against is not a bad commit but entropy: a convenient field added to a listing DTO, twelve tokens per row, three releases, entity-shaped JSON again. **Three payloads resist a fixed ceiling and are handled rather than ignored:** the context pack's `model` section describes the whole instance, so it is guarded **one type row at a time** (`context.type-row`), which is both order-independent and the better guard — a field added to the type shape multiplies by the size of somebody's content model; `conventions` is prose that grows with the instance and is bounded in production by `shio.agent.memory.*` instead; `diagnostics` is an in-memory window whose size is an operational fact, not a shape. Two of the three tests are claims rather than ceilings: **terse must cost less than JSON** (SH78's entire justification — if it ever inverts, the second encoding should be deleted rather than kept out of politeness) and **`ids=true` must cost meaningfully more** (so SH121's measurement stays a measurement rather than becoming folklore).
- **SH114** — **Instance memory / conventions store** (`GET/PUT/DELETE /api/v2/agent/memory`, `shio remember`, [ShAgentMemoryService](../shio-app/src/main/java/com/viglet/shio/api/agent/memory/ShAgentMemoryService.java), [ShAgentMemoryEntry](../shio-app/src/main/java/com/viglet/shio/persistence/model/agent/ShAgentMemoryEntry.java), `v2026.3.9.yaml`). The only piece in the block that **compounds**: everything else makes one session cheaper, a note makes every session after it cheaper. Keyed notes ("this site's blog uses `Article`, not `Post`") are served in the context pack's `conventions`, so the read path costs nothing — an agent that read the context has already read the memory. Five decisions worth keeping: (1) **a table, not content** — memory is read on the hot path, never delivered, and must survive a `prune`; modelled as content it would sit inside the very desired-state documents it exists to inform, and an agent that forgot to declare its own memory would delete it; (2) **upsert by `(tenant, scope, key)` with a unique index** — re-stating a convention rewrites one row instead of leaving the next session two near-duplicates to reconcile; (3) **`scope` is `''` for instance-wide, never `NULL`**, because SQL indexes do not treat `NULL`s as equal and a nullable scope would silently admit duplicates; (4) **attribution is a field, not a workflow** — every note names its author and the pack prints it, so a human's instruction and another agent's inference can be weighed differently, which is far cheaper than an approval queue for something that misleads the next session rather than changing the site (SH109 gates agent writes across the board); (5) **derived conventions are printed before remembered ones**, because a derived line is true by construction and a remembered one is somebody's claim. **No MCP tool**, deliberately: a tool schema is paid on every turn of every session (P3) and a coding agent has a shell, so `shio remember` costs nothing per turn and the context pack says it exists — which is also what makes the store self-sustaining. **SH160** is the open question for a client with no terminal. 12 tests.
- **SH115** — **`AGENTS.md` generator** (`?format=agents-md`, `shio context --as agents-md`, [ShAgentAgentsMd](../shio-app/src/main/java/com/viglet/shio/api/agent/ShAgentAgentsMd.java)). The same pack rendered as project agent instructions, for the moment *before* an agent has decided to work on content — a harness loads a file, it does not make a call. So the rendering is instruction-shaped rather than data-shaped: it opens with what to do, the model table exists to stop the agent inventing a post-type rather than to be a schema reference, and **individual pages are deliberately left out** (a generated file that lists content goes stale on the next publish and grows without bound; `find` answers "which pages" in one always-current call). It says out loud that it is generated and that the endpoint is the authority, and it carries the pack's digest so a reviewer can tell at a glance whether a checked-in file still matches the instance. Nothing measured is rendered — no token counts, no timestamps — because a generated file that changes on every run is a generated file nobody commits. One behaviour change came with it: an **unknown `format` is now a teaching 400** rather than a silent fallback to JSON, because with two renderings a typo cost a slightly wrong payload and with three, `agent-md` would quietly return JSON and the caller would conclude the feature does not exist.
- **SH116** — **Agent-read caching** ([ShAgentEtag](../shio-app/src/main/java/com/viglet/shio/api/agent/ShAgentEtag.java)). Strong ETags on the manifest, the context pack and the blueprint catalogue; `If-None-Match` on an unchanged instance answers **304**, which measures as **zero** on `X-Shio-Est-Tokens` — the assertion is on that number, because "re-reading the context is free" is either visible there or it is marketing. What this changes is a *decision*: re-checking the context was a trade (a few thousand tokens for certainty, or work from a remembered digest and risk being wrong) and is now the cheap default. **The tag is over a representation, not a state.** The SH77 digest deliberately covers content only, so JSON and terse share one — correct for "has anything changed?", wrong for `If-None-Match`, where a terse-cached client handed a JSON tag would keep the wrong bytes; every tag mixes the digest with `format` and `ids`. `Cache-Control: no-cache` (store it, but ask first) rather than a freshness lifetime, because content can change at any moment and revalidation costs a round trip and no tokens. Note what is *not* saved: the server still builds the pack to know its digest, and that is the right trade — the scarce resource is the caller's context window, and a cached digest that could go stale would break the only guarantee that makes the scheme usable.
- **SH127** — **Lean the delivery JSON and the SDK types, together** (`@JsonInclude(NON_NULL)` on the CDA read DTOs; `string | null` → `field?: string` in [shio-client/src/types.ts](../shio-client/src/types.ts); [ShCdaJsonLeanTest](../shio-app/src/test/java/com/viglet/shio/api/cda/ShCdaJsonLeanTest.java)). SH125 leaned the agent surface and stopped here on purpose: omitting a null while the published types still promised one would have handed every typed consumer an `undefined` from a comparison it believed was exhaustive — the payload gets smaller and the contract gets a lie in it. Both halves therefore moved in one commit. **The rule survives unchanged: NON_NULL, never NON_DEFAULT.** A null says nothing that absence does not already say; a `false` or a `0` frequently *is* the answer — `published:false` is the difference between a draft and a page nobody mentioned, and `totalPosts:0` answers "is this folder empty?". The visible payoff on the agent side is that the context pack's `model` section no longer inherits a null through the shared `ShCdaSchemaField` (P10 composition over a contract that could not be leaned unilaterally), and [ShAgentJsonLeanTest](../shio-app/src/test/java/com/viglet/shio/api/agent/ShAgentJsonLeanTest.java)'s characterization of that cost is **inverted rather than deleted**, so a null re-introduced on the delivery shape still surfaces at both ends.
- **SH157** — **Close the tool-call gap** ([ShAgentProofService](../shio-app/src/main/java/com/viglet/shio/api/agent/ShAgentProofService.java), [ShAgentContextSection](../shio-app/src/main/java/com/viglet/shio/api/agent/ShAgentContextSection.java), [ShAgentRoundTripTest](../shio-app/src/test/java/com/viglet/shio/api/agent/ShAgentRoundTripTest.java)). The benchmark's own verdict, acted on: tokens cleared the concept spec's ≈10× and round trips cleared nothing, and the traces said why — every canonical task opened with discovery (manifest, then context) and closed with proof (verify), and the work in between was one or two calls. **The framing was the remaining round trips**, so both ends fold in and both are opt-in.
  <br>**Discovery in one call.** `GET /agent/context?include=all,manifest` carries the manifest's `features`, `limits` and `startHere` in a `capabilities` section. **The endpoint index deliberately stays behind** — it is ~87% of the manifest, it changes only when the build does, and it is exactly what SH116's ETag already makes free; folding it in would re-send it every time a post changed. Three rules: `manifest` is **the one section that must be named**, so `include=all` still means all the sections of the *context pack* and no session pays for a document it already holds; the capabilities are attached **after the digest is taken**, because the digest answers "has the content changed" and a build number moving it would send every agent re-reading every sitemap after an upgrade; and `all` became a **token** inside the list rather than only a whole value, since `all,manifest` is the natural spelling and the manifest's own example shows it.
  <br>**A write that returns its own proof.** `?verify=true` on `/agent/batch` and `/agent/apply` runs the SH99 lint over exactly the addresses the run touched and returns it as `proof`. It is strictly better than the separate verify it replaces — scoped to the change instead of to the site — and it runs **after** the write transaction commits, which is what living outside the write service buys: inside it, the lint would read state a rollback is about to discard, and a read failure could fail a write that had already succeeded. **Attribution is the part that could mislead**, so an op that wrote no fields (a `publish` on a post nobody edited) has its address named: a finding against it predates the run. Those notes are emitted only when there *are* findings — explaining that none of zero findings were caused by the run is prose P3 says to stop paying for. A **dry run gets no proof**: linting a state the plan has not created yet would read as "the plan is clean". `shio_write` takes the argument for ~15 tokens; `shio_apply` could not, at 457 measured against a 460 per-tool ceiling (**SH227**).
  <br>**Two defects found while measuring it.** The context pack's ETag **did not include `include`** — three blocks after SH116 wrote down the rule it breaks — so `include=model` and the whole pack shared a tag off the same digest, and a caller could revalidate the first against the second's cache and keep a pack with no sitemap in it (**SH229** wants the lint). And `/agent/batch` had **no `format=terse`**, the only part of this namespace without one: `ShAgentReadTerse.changes` has rendered change sets for MCP since SH83 and only the REST endpoints could not ask for it. That mattered here, because paying for the proof in JSON while the verify it replaced could be terse trades one target for the other. A third, smaller one went with them: `shio_write`'s terse output dropped the SH108 confirm token, so an MCP client could never complete a delete.
  <br>**What it measured.** Every task lost a call: **tool calls 2.3×–3.8×**, up from 1.7×–3.2×. Tokens moved both ways and the detail is the point — `build-marketing-site` nearly halved (4459 → 2375) because the manifest read it dropped was the single most expensive call on the whole agent path, while `fix-broken-link` went 306 → 364 because the attached proof genuinely costs more than the terse re-verify it replaced. **That trade is stated rather than hidden**: a round trip bought with a few tokens. The floors in [token-budgets.properties](../shio-app/src/test/resources/token-budgets.properties) **rise** with the measurement — the first time in that file it has moved in that direction, and the first change in three blocks to move a ratio by improving the agent path rather than by the baseline getting leaner.
- **SH158** — **Guard the request-reading config against test/prod drift** ([ShRequestReadingConfigLintTest](../shio-app/src/test/java/com/viglet/shio/spring/ShRequestReadingConfigLintTest.java), [ShMinimalRequestBodyTest](../shio-app/src/test/java/com/viglet/shio/api/agent/ShMinimalRequestBodyTest.java)). Two guards for the *class* of defect SH112 tripped over rather than the instance. The **lint** reads both `application.properties` files and fails the build when a key governing how a request is parsed and bound is set in production and absent from the test override — which shadows the main file rather than merging with it, so a misconfiguration there is invisible to every test *because the tests are the thing that is misconfigured*. The prefix list (`spring.jackson.deserialization.`, `.mapper.`, `.parser.`, `spring.servlet.multipart.`) is the whole definition and is deliberately narrow: serialization is out, because a test asserting on a response object never went through the writer. It found two real gaps the day it was written — `DEFAULT_VIEW_INCLUSION`, and the multipart limits, which meant every SH38 upload test was proving Spring's 1 MB default rather than the subsystem. The **minimal-body test** sends the shortest documented JSON to each of seven write surfaces and asserts only that Spring did not raise `HttpMessageNotReadableException` — not a status code, because a minimal body naturally lands on a business outcome and pinning that would make the class break on unrelated rule changes. The distinction it draws is the one that matters: *"I could not read what you sent"* is a different failure from *"I read it and it is wrong"*, and only the first is invisible to every other test in the repository.
- **SH159** — **Conditional reads for the rest of the surface** ([ShAgentBodyEtag](../shio-app/src/main/java/com/viglet/shio/api/agent/ShAgentBodyEtag.java), [ShAgentBodyConditionalReadTest](../shio-app/src/test/java/com/viglet/shio/api/agent/ShAgentBodyConditionalReadTest.java)). `find`, `read`, `changes` and the SH16 post-type listing answer `304`, which measures **zero** on `X-Shio-Est-Tokens`. These are the reads an agent makes *repeatedly* — `find` at the top of a loop, `changes` as the poll whose honest answer is usually "nothing", the post-type list on every `push --check` and every console editor load. **The tag is over the rendered body**, unlike SH116's: those three discovery reads each knew their own content digest and these four do not, and four hand-derived digests would be four things that can quietly disagree with what was actually sent — a digest that is *almost* right answers `304` to a caller holding different bytes, with no way for it to find out. Hashing the bytes is exact by construction and gets the representation rule for free: a two-field projection and a whole document are different bytes, so nobody has to remember to mix `fields` into the tag. Rendering happens once — the serialized string is what is hashed *and* what is returned, so a `200` costs what it always did. **One defect fixed to make it possible:** the change feed's lag note embedded the computed ceiling instant (`now - lagMillis`), so every `changes` response was different bytes from the last one — on the endpoint whose entire job is to be polled — while telling the caller nothing it could act on, since the actionable number is the lag and that is a constant. `changes` revalidates in **cursor** mode and not in window mode, which is correct rather than a gap: without `since` the response's own cursor is the moving edge of the feed (**SH232**).
- **SH160** — **Memory for a client with no shell** ([ShRememberTool](../shio-app/src/main/java/com/viglet/shio/api/agent/mcp/tools/ShRememberTool.java)). The decision SH114 deferred, made: **an eleventh MCP tool**, `shio_remember`. SH114's argument was right for Claude Code — a schema is paid on every turn, a coding agent has a terminal, `shio remember` costs nothing per turn — and wrong for a pure MCP client, which could *read* the memory (the notes ride in the context pack for free) and had no way to write one, so `instanceMemory: true` was a half-truth for exactly the clients the manifest exists to inform. **P1 beats P3 here because of what was missing**: the memory is the only mechanism in the product that makes session N+1 cheaper than session N, and it is write-once-read-many, so a store nobody can write to stays empty and the free read returns nothing. The two cheaper shapes were considered and rejected — a `remember` property on `shio_write` costs a third as much and **does not deliver the capability**, because most conclusions worth keeping are reached while *reading* and there is no write to hang them on; reporting the gap as a manifest flag announces a hole rather than closing one. Forgetting gets no tool of its own: an empty note deletes, the convention `PUT /agent/memory` already uses, so the delete costs no schema at all. The description was trimmed 167 → 128 **before** `mcp.tools.list.total` moved 2200 → 2360, which is the order these raises should happen in. The context pack's derived line now names the tool first, since it is read by the clients that have no shell.
